The reactions consisted of 1X SYBR Green mix (Maxima SYBR Green qPCR Master Mix, Fermentas), 10 µM of each of the primers F and R, 1 µl of cDNA and 4 µl of sterile water completing a total volume of 14 µl. The reactions were performed under the following conditions: 50°C for 2 min, 95°C for 10 min, 40 cycles at 95°C for 15 s and 60°C for 1 min. Fluorescence readings were always taken at this last step.

After finishing the reaction cycles, the specificity of the products was checked by running a dissociation curve analysis protocol, starting at 95°C for 15 s, 60°C for 1 min and 95°C for 15 s. Data were collected in the last two steps. Criteria for primer quality were a single peak of dissociation and amplification efficiencies between 80–110%.

The quantification of lncov1 transcript levels was done on cDNA samples of ovaries dissected from worker larvae in the fourth instar (L4), and the substages of the fifth instar covering the feeding (L5F1–L5F3) and the cocoon spinning phases (L5S1–L5S3). Three independent biological samples were prepared for each stage, each consisting of 15 pairs of ovaries. Each biological sample was analyzed in technical triplicates. Transcript abundance for lncov1 and the reference gene actin, validated for RT-qPCR assays in honey bees [70], were expressed as Ct values (threshold cycle). Relative expression levels of lncov1 were expressed as 2−ΔΔCt [71] in relation to L4 transcript levels.

For the statistical analysis of expression, the 2−ΔΔCt values for the developmental stages were log transformed and analyzed with a Kruskal-Wallis test followed by post hoc Dunn's Multiple Comparison testing, these implemented in GraphPad Prism v 4.0. The level of significance considered was P≤0.05.

In situ localization of lncov1 transcripts was analyzed in ovaries of worker larvae in the late feeding stage (L5F3). Antisense and sense probes were synthesized using lncov1 specific primers containing a T7 promoter sequence (underlined) at the respective 5′ends (11.31FT7 5′-TAATACGACTCACTATAGGGCTGAGTTTCGGGTGTGTGAGG-3′; 11.31RT7 5′-TAATACGACTCACTATAGGGCTGAGTTTCGGGTGTGAGG-3′) in combination with the corresponding primers lacking this T7 sequence (11.31F and 11.31R). Amplification parameters were 94°C for 2 min, 40 cycles of 94°C for 45 s, 60°C for 45 s, 72°C for 1 min, and a final extension step of 72°C for 10 min. The fragments generated for the 11.31 primer combinations (11.31FT7+11.31R and 11.31RT7+11.31F) had a product length of 151 bp. The amplification products were checked in an agarose gel, purified (Illustra GFX PCR DNA and Gel Band Purification kit, GE Healthcare) and quantified spectrophotometrically. Subsequently, RNA probes were generated from these products by in vitro transcription from the T7 promoter using a FISH Tag RNA kit (Invitrogen).

The ovaries were processed following the fluorescent in situ hybridization procedure described for Drosophila melanogaster ovaries [72]. Briefly, the fixed ovaries were hydrated first in methanol, then with a mixture of methanol/PTw (PBS 1%, Tween 0.1%), and finally 3 X with PTw. The material was transferred to a DMSO 1∶9 PPTwT solution (PTw, paraformaldehyde 4%, Triton ×100 0,1%) for 20 min at room temperature. After five washes in PTw, they were incubated for 30 s with protease K (40 µg/mL) and again washed with glycine (10 mg/mL) in PTw. Following two washes with PTw they were re-fixed with PPTwT and washed 5× in PTw. Before hybridization, the ovaries were incubated for 10 min in PTw/HS (50% formamide, 4X SSC, 50 µg/mL heparin, 1X Denhardt's solution, 250 µg/mL yeast RNA, 500 µg/mL salmon testes DNA), and another 10 min with HS alone. After 1 h at 45°C in new HS the fluorescent RNA probe was added and hybridization proceeded for 16 h at 45°C. The RNA probe had been synthesized with the FISH Tag RNA kit (Invitrogen), following the manufacturer's instructions. Subsequently, the labeled ovaries were washed twice with HS and sequentially with HS/PTw (3∶1), HS/PTw (1∶1), HS/PTw (1∶3) and PTw. Nuclei were labeled with DAPI/PTw (4000∶1) and images of 0.5 or 1 µm optical sections were captured by laser confocal microscopy in a TCS-SP5 System (Leica). Leica LAS-AF software was used for image acquisition and processing. No adjustments were made with respect to image brightness and/or contrast.

title: Social interactions affecting caste development through physiological actions in termites
abstract: A colony of social insects is not only an aggregation of individuals but also a functional unit. To achieve adaptive social behavior in fluctuating environmental conditions, in addition to coordination of physiological status in each individual, the whole colony is coordinated by interactions among colony members. The study on the regulation of social-insect colonies is termed “social physiology.” Termites, a major group of social insects, exhibit many interesting phenomena related to social physiology, such as mechanisms of caste regulation in a colony. In their colonies, there are different types of individuals, i.e., castes, which show distinctive phenotypes specialized in specific colony tasks. Termite castes comprise reproductives, soldiers and workers, and the caste composition can be altered depending on circumstances. For the regulation of caste compositions, interactions among individuals, i.e., social interactions, are thought to be important. In this article, we review previous studies on the adaptive meanings and those on the proximate mechanisms of the caste regulation in termites, and try to understand those comprehensively in terms of social physiology. Firstly, we summarize classical studies on the social interactions. Secondly, previous studies on the pheromone substances that mediate the caste regulatory mechanisms are overviewed. Then, we discuss the roles of a physiological factor, juvenile hormone (JH) in the regulation of caste differentiation. Finally, we introduce the achievements of molecular studies on the animal sociality (i.e., sociogenomics) in terms of social physiology. By comparing the proximate mechanisms of social physiology in termites with those in hymenopterans, we try to get insights into the general principles of social physiology in social animals.
body_text:
“Physiology” refers to biological studies that deal with the functions and activities of living things. Most of physiological studies focus on the mechanisms in an individual or part(s) of an individual (e.g., Randall et al., 2002). However, physiological events are not necessarily limited to within an individual, but may also involve interactions with environments surrounding the individual. In some organisms, by interacting and cooperating with other individuals of the same species, a sophisticated entity is constructed at a higher dimension than the individual level. Such an entity is often referred to as a “society” (Wilson, 1975), and a number of studies on social organisms, particularly social insects, have been performed. During the last two decades, the term “social physiology” was proposed to describe the study that tried to understand communication systems that facilitate colony activities (Seeley, 1995).

A colony of social insects is often referred to as a “superorganism” as if it were one individual (Hölldobler and Wilson, 2008). As this name suggests, colonies can change their inner conditions through various actions performed by colony members. These performances by colony members can be divided into two types of actions: the actions of each individual (division of labor) and the interactions between colony members (communications). Two study areas, i.e., social anatomy and social physiology, that were firstly classified by Johnson and Linksvayer (2010) respectively focus on the proximate factors responsible for the two types of actions. They also argued that these two types of studies should be deeply connected to each other although studies on social physiology were delayed compared to social anatomy. Furthermore, studies in social physiology have been concentrated especially in social hymenopterans, i.e., ants, bees and social wasps (Seeley, 1995; Pankiw, 2004; Johnson and Linksvayer, 2010). However, this study area should include examples in broad range of animal groups in order to elucidate the principles of social physiology. In that sense, another major eusocial insect group, termites, should also be focused as the study materials of social physiology.

Castes, one of the distinctive features of social insects, possess morphologies specialized in tasks which are allocated in a colony (Wilson, 1971). The regulatory mechanisms optimizing caste ratios, including behavioral castes, is an essential focus in social physiology because it maximizes the colony productivity (Johnson and Linksvayer, 2010). To discuss caste regulatory mechanisms, termites are an interesting group due to a number of their conspicuous characteristics (Howard and Thorne, 2011). For example, termites construct diverse, huge, and complex nests, which include enormous numbers of individuals (Wilson, 1971; Noirot and Darlington, 2000). In termites, therefore, there must be distinctive mechanisms to coordinate such huge colonies, in comparison with those of social hymenopterans. Furthermore, termites possess the soldier caste, that is distinctive among social insects due to their developmental status and specialized morphologies (Deligne et al., 1981; Roisin, 2000). The soldier caste is thought to be an immature (non-imago) stage, probably due to the hemimetabolous caste developmental pathways (Eggleton, 2011) in termites, while social hymenopterans are holometabolous (Miura, 2004). Thus, although social hymenopterans have provided us implications, distinctive characteristics in termites will also provide new insights into the principles of social physiology.

In this article, we aim to overview the knowledge on the proximate mechanisms of caste regulations in termites as an example of social physiology, especially focusing on the soldier differentiation. We would like to discuss this issue along the biological events that occur in termite colonies and inside the focal individuals: from the communications among colony members, via physiological actions, affecting the developmental events. Furthermore, the molecules responsible for these processes are also focused.

Caste differentiation in social insects is a representative case of polyphenism, in which multiple discrete phenotypes are seen in a single species (Nijhout, 1999, 2003). Castes of termites are primarily divided into two types of individuals: fertile (reproductives) and sterile individuals (neuters) (Thorne, 1996; Roisin, 2000). The sterile castes include workers, presoldiers and soldiers, while the fertile ones are alates, primary reproductives and secondary reproductives (Figure 1). Alates with imaginal characteristics (i.e., wings, testes, ovaries) that develop during the nymphal stages perform nuptial flights, shed their wings, mate, found new colonies, and then become primary reproductives (i.e., kings and queens). When primary reproductives die or become scenescent, or when colonies expand, some individuals differentiate into the secondary reproductives.

Representative caste developmental patterns in termites. (A) Linear pathway. (B) Bifurcated pathway. Arrowheads indicate mating and oviposition. White and black arrows indicate hatching and molts, respectively. Not all pseudergates or workers molt into subsequent developmental stages.

In contrast, soldiers and workers are sterile castes not engaged in reproduction. Late-stage larvae that behave as workers are called as “pseudergates” in the relatively basal termite lineages (Thorne, 1996). In this review, we will expediently use the term “worker” including pseudergate sensu lato (Korb and Hartfelder, 2008; Roisin and Korb, 2011). A part of workers differentiate into soldiers with drastic morphological modifications. A soldier possesses a pair of extremely elongated mandibles and/or a frontal projection with an exocrine gland from which defensive substances are discharged (Noirot, 1969; Weesner, 1969).

Depending on the species, the developmental pathways are roughly divided into two patterns, i.e., a linear pathway or a bifurcated pathway (Roisin, 2000; Bourguignon et al., 2009; Figure 1). Basically, all larvae hatched from eggs have the potential to develop into any castes. Classically, assuming that all egg contains the similar or identical genetic information, caste developmental fates are determined depending on various environmental factors experienced during postembryonic development, as well as sex and egg factors (Noirot, 1990, 1991). Major environmental stimuli include nutritional and seasonal factors such as temperature and humidity (Noirot, 1991; Fei and Henderson, 2002; Liu et al., 2005; Scharf et al., 2007). Termites can receive these stimuli by themselves, and in some cases, this environmental information can be transferred through social interactions such as allogrooming and/or trophallaxis, the latter of which is the exchange of nutritious food by stomodeal (i.e., oral) or proctodeal (i.e., anal) transfer (Noirot, 1991; Tarver et al., 2011). However, little is known about the relationships between environmental factors and patterns of social interactions (e.g., Machida et al., 2001).

Except for environmental stimuli, sexes are also important factors for the caste differentiation (Noirot, 1990). Termites show the XY sex determination system (Matsuura, 2011), and neuter castes are specialized in or biased toward either sex in some species (Roisin, 2000). For instance, in the genus Nasutitermes only male workers differentiated into soldiers (Hojo et al., 2004). In addition, a candidate X-chromosome-linked gene, worker, is reported to affect the caste differentiation in Reticulitermes speratus (Hayashi et al., 2007). The worker is hypothesized to have two alleles (wkA and wkB). They reported that male (XY) larvae possessing wkA were destined to be workers, while in female (XX), heterozygous in worker locus determined the differentiation into workers. Larvae with other genotypes basically develop into nymphs although only the genotype for females with homozygous wkB is thought to be lethal. This is the first report showing a genetic influence in reproductive division of labor (Kitade et al., 2011). However, it should also be noted that the caste fates are also affected by coexisting castes (Hayashi et al., 2007), suggesting that, except for environmental cues, social interaction among castes (or phenotypes) is the major factor affecting the caste composition in termites. The abnormal caste ratios set by artificial manipulations were gradually returned to the normal caste ratios just by keeping those colonies under laboratory conditions (Lefeuve and Bordereau, 1984; Mao et al., 2005; Park and Raina, 2005). These experiments were performed under laboratory conditions where environmental conditions were stable, so that the changes of social interactions are suggested to be the important factors adjusting the caste ratio.

Historically, studies on the caste ratio regulations in termites started with the reports on seasonal transitions of caste composition in some species, such as Odontotermes redemanni (Banerjee, 1966) and Trinervitermes ebenerianus (Sands, 1965). Howard and Haverty (1981) found that, in Reticulitermes flavipes, the caste proportion in a colony changed with seasons. They reported that the soldier ratios increased concurrently with temperature and peaked when alate differentiation was about to occur. Furthermore, the ratios of soldiers and reproductives were kept at a low level (2 and 0.1%, respectively, on average during a year). Generally, as reviewed by Haverty (1977) on 112 termite species, the proportion of soldiers in a colony is low in all the investigated species.

In social hymenopterans, the low proportion of reproductive castes was often discussed in terms of conflicts among colony members (Bourke and Franks, 1961). Conflict among reproductives is also suggested to exist in termite sociality since the artificial addition of extra reproductives resulted in cannibalism among reproductives (Lüscher, 1961). In contrast, the adaptive meaning of low soldier proportion has been discussed based on the results of experimental manipulations. Basically, a colony needs soldiers because soldier is the only caste that can intercept attacks by enemies (mainly predators) (Noirot and Darlington, 2000). However, the possession of soldiers in colonies should incur some costs, since soldiers cannot feed by themselves but require help from workers (Noirot and Darlington, 2000; Korb and Hartfelder, 2008). Actually, an excess of soldiers caused high mortality of nestmates in Coptotermes formosanus (Haverty, 1979). Thus, maintaining the appropriate proportion of soldiers is necessary for termite colonies. However, only a few studies on the adaptive significance of caste proportion have been reported in termites.

The most famous discoveries on the regulatory mechanisms of reproductive caste differentiation in termites were a series of studies on the differentiation of secondary reproductives of Kalotermes flavicollis performed by Lüscher (1952, 1961) in the middle of 20th century. He clarified the developmental pathway of the focal species and the fact that workers had the potential to differentiate into both secondary reproductives and soldiers. Moreover, his subsequent studies revealed that workers differentiated into secondary reproductives or soldiers after the removal of primary reproductives or soldiers, respectively, from the colony (Lüscher, 1960, 1961, 1974). These results suggested that the caste differentiation was repressively regulated by other colony members (castes) probably through pheromones. Furthermore, the differentiation of secondary reproductives was not inhibited when the anus of primary reproductives was sealed, indicating that some substances were transferred through proctodeal trophallaxis (Lüscher, 1955, 1974). In K. flavicollis, fewer alates were differentiated when nymphs were isolated with the royal pair than in groups of orphan nymphs (Springhetti, 1969, 1971, 1972). This inhibitory effect occurred only when the king and queen had directly contacted with nymphs, suggesting that the direct communications such as stomodeal and/or proctodeal trophallaxis, or grooming would be responsible for it.

In contrast to the inhibitory effects of primary reproductives, the alate production was shown to be accelerated by the presence of soldiers in Zootermopsis nevadensis (Lüscher, 1975). Similarly, the differentiation of secondary reproductives of K. flavicollis was accelerated by soldiers (Springhetti, 1969). Both cases indicate that the differentiation to reproductives seemed to be induced by the presence of soldiers (Figure 2).

Summary of the regulation of caste differentiation by social interactions. Differentiation into reproductives and soldiers (bold arrows) are stimulated by different castes (thin arrows) and inhibited by the same castes (broken arrows). Note that the effect of secondary reproductives on soldier differentiation is still an open question (see text for details).

The inhibition of soldier differentiation by soldiers was first reported in incipient colonies of Z. angusticollis. Most of the incipient colonies possessed only one soldier for a long time. Castle (1934) discovered that, when a soldier was introduced into another incipient colony before the first soldier was differentiated, soldier differentiation was suppressed. When the soldier was removed from an incipient colony, another workers started to differentiate into a new soldiers. By using individuals collected from mature colonies, the inhibitory effects of soldiers on the additional soldier differentiation were demonstrated in K. flavicollis (Figure 2) (Springhetti, 1969, 1985). Lefeuve and Bordereau (1984) firstly reported the chemical characteristics of soldier pheromone using Nasutitermes lujae. They revealed that not only living soldiers but also chemical components extracted from soldiers using organic solvent inhibited the soldier differentiation. These inhibitory effects did not occur unless workers directly contacted with the soldier extracts, suggesting that the pheromone suppressing additional soldier differentiation was a non-volatile, non-polar substance. Furthermore, Okot-Kotber et al. (1991) reported that soldier extracts of Reticulitermes flavipes inhibited soldier differentiation in termite species belonging to a different family, suggesting that the inhibitory mechanisms are shared among termite lineages.

On the other hand, in N. lujae and Cubitermes fungifaber, the soldier differentiation occurred more frequently in the groups of workers reared with primary reproductives than those without reproductives (Bordereau and Han, 1986). Similar effects of reproductives on the additional soldier differentiation were found in K. flavicollis (Springhetti, 1969, 1970) and Z. nevadensis (Maekawa et al., 2012). Generally in termites, the soldier differentiation is stimulated by the presence of primary reproductives and suppressed by other soldiers (Figure 2). The presence of secondary reproductives is thought to stimulate the soldier differentiation as well as primary reproductives, although the direct evidences have not been reported. In general, the caste differentiation appears to be inhibited by the same caste while induced by a different caste, probably through pheromone actions (Bordereau, 1985; Noirot, 1991).

The term “pheromone” was firstly defined by Karlson and Lüscher (1959), who suggested that, in termites, some substances inhibit the additional differentiation of secondary reproductives, which was repressed by interactions between primary reproductives and workers. Since then, the pheromones controlling caste differentiation in termites had not been identified. However, recent techniques of chemical analyses applied to ecological phenomenon have contributed to the identification of caste-regulating pheromones in termites. For example, n-butyl-n-butyrate and 2-methyl-1-butanol were reported as the essential components of queen pheromones in R. speratus (Matsuura et al., 2010).

For the soldier differentiation, two related terpenoids were identified as dominant components from the soldier head extracts in R. flavipes: γ-cadinene and its aldehyde, γ-cadinenal (Tarver et al., 2009). The subsequent analyses revealed that γ-cadinenal worked as a pheromone inhibiting the soldier differentiation (so-called “soldier pheromone”) and γ-cadinene as a pheromone promoting the soldier differentiation (Tarver et al., 2011). However, these candidate pheromone substances were not detected from some populations of the focal species, suggesting that the synthesis of these substances depends on populations and/or seasons (Perdereau et al., 2010). In addition to these, β-selinene was identified as a major compound in the soldier head extracts in R. speratus acting as an aggregation pheromone for colony members (Nguyen et al., 2011). They suggested that this substance might be involved in the inhibition of soldier differentiation from workers because the interactions among colony members might be accelerated by aggregation. Actually, the direct contact of soldiers with workers inhibits the additional soldier differentiation from workers in Coptotermes formosanus (Park and Raina, 2003; Dong et al., 2009).

Recent advances in chemical analyses have eventually enabled us to identify queen and soldier pheromones in termites that were predicted by Karlson and Lüscher (1959). These advances will accelerate researches on the regulatory mechanisms of caste ratio. In future studies, many other functional compounds will be identified, so that it will be possible to examine the regulatory mechanisms by those pheromone chemicals, including the downstream reception and endocrinological pathways, are universal across termite taxa.

Early studies demonstrated that the transplantation of corpora allata (CA; juvenile hormone-producing endocrine glands) induced caste differentiation of recipient workers in K. flavicollis (Lüscher, 1952, 1960). CA from soldiers, reproductives and late-stage nymphs induced the soldier differentiation, whereas CA from workers and early-stage nymphs induced the differentiation into reproductives. These results suggest that juvenile hormone (JH) plays important roles in the caste differentiation, and the JH synthesis activity in CA differs among castes. In addition to the CA transplantation, the applications of ectopic JH analogs (JHAs) to workers also induced the soldier differentiation in many termite species, indicating that an increase in JH titer stimulated differentiation into soldiers (Howard and Haverty, 1979). Thus, JH has been recognized as the most important endocrine factor for caste differentiation, and a model of caste differentiation by JH action was proposed, in which high JH titer induces soldier differentiation whereas low JH titer causes differentiation into alates (Nijhout and Wheeler, 1982; Figure 3).

Schematic drawings of classical (Nijhout and Wheeler, 1982; left) and recent (Cornette et al., 2008; right) models on the transitions of JH titer (vertical axis) during intermolt period of pseudergate (horizontal axis) before caste differentiation. Caste names at the far left indicate the future castes determined by the JH patterns. According to Cornette et al. (2008), changes in JH titers during the pseudergate stage before the differentiation into soldiers or alates were consistent with classical models. There were some differences between the model and measured titers in the case of stationary molts.

Although classical studies suggested that the patterns of JH-titer transitions during intermolt determined the future caste differentiation, precise measurements of JH titer were not performed until the establishment of JH quantification methods (Zera, 2007). So far, three major methods for JH quantification have been reported: radioimmunoassay (Greenberg and Tobe, 1985; Goodman et al., 1990), gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) (Shu et al., 1997), liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) (Westerlund and Hoffmann, 2004). The JH quantification by GC-MS was developed earlier than those using LC-MS. For the JH quantification to be a routine lab procedure, however, GC-MS analysis has some disadvantages due to the requirement of many samples and mass consumption of harmful organic solvents for sample preparation (Bergot et al., 1981; Rembold and Lackner, 1985). Recently, a rapid and accurate method for JH quantification by LC-MS was developed to quantify insect JHs (e.g., JHI, II, and III) and their metabolites (Westerlund and Hoffmann, 2004). By applying this method, Cornette et al. (2008) and Gotoh et al. (2008) established the quantification of JH titers in a termite Hodotermopsis sjostedti. Cornette et al. (2008) further analyzed the patterns of JH titers during differentiation into reproductives and soldiers in H. sjostedti, indicating that JH titers of pseudergates prior to soldier differentiation were constantly high, whereas, those of nymphs before molts into alates remained low (Figure 3). These two JH transitions leading to the soldier and alate differentiations are consistent with the patterns proposed by Nijhout and Wheeler (1982), although there are minor differences in the patterns leading to the stationary molt (repeating the same instar) to pseudergates (Figure 3). It was also demonstrated that JH titers of nymphs before alate differentiation were low in Cryptotermes secundus (Korb et al., 2009a) and Reticulitermes speratus (Maekawa et al., 2010).

As for the regulations of the hemolymphatic JH titer in insects, it is known that JH titer is not only regulated by the activity of JH synthesis in CA and secretion from CA, but also by other biological processes such as sequestration and degradation (Gilbert et al., 2000; Nation, 2008). Actually, the transcription levels of hexamerins (a factor related to JH sequestration) were shown to be up-regulated during soldier differentiation (Scharf et al., 2005, 2007; Cornette et al., 2013), so that the sequestration process is suggested to modify JH titer during the caste differentiation.

Based on the fact that JH is the most important factor involved in the caste differentiation in termites, it was considered that the JH actions mediate the effects of interactions among colony members on the caste differentiation (Henderson, 1998). By applying the technique of GC-MS analysis in Coptotermes formosanus, it was shown that the isolation of workers from soldiers increased the worker JH titers, suggesting that the presence of soldiers may repress the JH titer of nestmates (Mao et al., 2005; Park and Raina, 2005). Since these studies did not employ the application of JH or JH analogs, the observed effects were suggested to occur under natural conditions.

The JH quantification method by LC-MS that was performed in H. sjostedti (Cornette et al., 2003) was also applied to analyze precise effects of the soldier presence on worker JH titers during the soldier differentiation in R. speratus (Watanabe et al., 2011; Figure 4). The results of this study in which JH titers of JH-treated workers reared with/without soldiers were quantified (Figure 4A), revealed that, under the absence of soldiers, the JH application rapidly increased the worker JH titers (Figure 4B), resulting in the elevation of presoldier differentiation ratio from workers (Figure 4C). On the other hand, under the presence of soldiers, the rapid increase in worker JH titers by JH application was suppressed (Figure 4B), leading to the low induction rates (Figure 4C). These results suggested that the soldier differentiation triggered by the JH application was suppressed by the soldier presence, probably by lowering the worker JH titer. This suppression by the soldier presence occurred very rapidly (within a few days), suggesting the rapid and accurate regulation of soldier-caste ratio in termites.

A study examining the relationship between social interactions and JH titers in termites (Watanabe et al., 2011). (A) Experimental designs to obtain workers (white arrowheads) under the absence/presence of soldiers (black arrowhead) put on petri dishes with filter papers containing JHIII. The JH titers of workers reared by this method were quantified along the time course. (B) JH-titer transitions in workers during the soldier induction experiment. (C) Induction rates of presoldier differentiation under the absence/presence of soldiers. The gray shading indicates the range of soldier ratio observed in nature.

Extremely elongated mandibles used to bite or flick enemies (mechanical defense), or frontal glands discharging aversive and/or toxic substances (chemical defense) toward enemies (Deligne et al., 1981; Prestwich, 1984) were formed through the distinctive morphogenetic events during the process of soldier differentiation (Noirot, 1969; Weesner, 1969). This process can be induced artificially by using JH or JHA, which initiates the soldier differentiation (Miura et al., 2003; Šobotník et al., 2010).

In order to examine the relationship between JH titer and mandibular length, various concentrations of JH were applied to workers in Reticulitermes speratus, in which soldiers possess elongated mandibles (Tsuchiya et al., 2008; Figures 5A,B). The results showed that mandibular lengths of induced presoldiers depended on the concentrations of applied JH. Namely, higher concentrations of JH induced presoldiers with longer mandibles while lower concentrations induced presoldiers with shorter mandibles. Interestingly, the resultant mandibular lengths were also affected by the presence of soldiers even under the same JH concentration; workers coexisted with soldiers molted to presoldiers with shorter mandibles while those without soldiers molted to presoldiers with longer mandibles. These results strongly suggest that the presence of soldiers affects the developmental processes in the soldier differentiation by controlling JH titer (Tsuchiya et al., 2008). Actually, a subsequent work quantifying the endogenous JH titer in the same species supported this idea (Watanabe et al., 2011).

The soldier effects on morphogenesis shown by Tsuchiya et al. (2008) and Watanabe and Maekawa (2012). (A) Illustrations of a soldier and a worker of Reticulitermes speratus. (B) Mandibles of a worker (left) and a soldier (right). (C) A Median section of a soldier. The frontal gland invaginates into the head and thorax (indicated by pink). (D) Relationships between the effects of soldier presence and the JH titers of workers. When the soldier effect is weak, the JH titer rises resulting in the elongation of mandibles. Under the strong soldier effect, low JH titer repress the mandibular elongation.

In some species of rhinotermitids, the frontal gland seen in soldiers (Figure 5C) is also formed during the soldier differentiation induced by JH applications (Lelis and Everaerts, 1993; Watanabe and Maekawa, 2008; Šobotník et al., 2010). In R. speratus, Watanabe and Maekawa (2012) showed that the degree of frontal-gland formation depended on the concentrations of applied JH; higher JH concentration induced well-developed glands whereas lower one did not. It was also suggested that the soldier presence suppressed the frontal-gland formation via the regulation of JH titer (Figure 5D). These studies focusing on the development of soldier characters indicated that interactions among individuals did not only affect the caste differentiation but also the caste-specific morphogenesis. In these cases, JH titers in workers might be suppressed to lower levels by the presence of soldiers (Figure 5D). Since the social interactions are suggested to affect the expression patterns of genes that were shown to regulate the soldier-specific morphogenesis (Koshikawa et al., 2002, 2003, 2005, 2010; Hattori et al., 2013; Toga et al., 2012, 2013), the relationships between those gene expression patterns and social interactions will be clarified sooner or later.

During the last decade, many pioneering works in termites related to the new study area “sociogenomics” have been reported (Robinson, 1999; Robinson et al., 2005). By large-scale gene expression analyses (such as differential display, macro-array, cDNA subtraction and representation difference analysis) followed by functional assays such as RNA interference (RNAi), the proximate mechanisms of caste differentiation have been extensively analyzed, leading to the identifications of genes involved in the termite sociality (Miura and Scharf, 2011). These can be the candidate factors involved in the social interactions affecting the caste differentiation.

The caste-specific gene that was firstly identified is Soldier-specific protein 1 (SOL1) in Hodotermopsis sjostedti, that was expressed exclusively in soldiers (Miura et al., 1999). Although the function of SOL1 remains unknown, the encoded protein belongs to the lipocalin protein family (Miura, 2004, 2005; Flower, 2000). Considering the general functions of lipocalins in signal transductions, there is a possibility that SOL1 might be involved in communications among colony members such as a carrier of soldier pheromone (Miura and Scharf, 2011).

Among genes involved in JH-related pathway, hexamerins and cytochrome P450s are well studied (Miura and Scharf, 2011). Hexamerins are one of the groups of JH-binding proteins (Gilbert et al., 2000), and hexamerin (Hex) genes were expressed prominently in fat bodies of workers during the soldier differentiation in Reticulitermes flavipes (Scharf et al., 2005; Zhou et al., 2006a). The Hex-knockdown by RNAi induced the soldier differentiation, suggesting that Hex genes play an important role in the soldier differentiation, by regulating JH titer in workers (Zhou et al., 2006b). Also in Hodotermopsis sjostedti, the Hex expressions were up-regulated in the course of soldier differentiation (Cornette et al., 2013), suggesting that hexamerin-based regulatory mechanisms of JH are widespread in termites. Cytochrome P450s are heme-containing oxidative enzymes which catalyze the syntheses and metabolisms of JHs as well as those of ecdysteroids and some pheromones in insects (Feyereisen, 1999; Scott and Wen, 2001). The expression levels of cytochrome P450 genes significantly up-regulated during the soldier differentiation in H. sjostedti (Cornette et al., 2006) and R. flavipes (Zhou et al., 2006c). Therefore, hexamerins and P450s can be candidate mediators between social interactions and physiological influences, as a study suggested that hexamerins played a role in the JH-titer regulation under the influences of nutritional and temperature conditions (Scharf et al., 2007).

Recently, a gene, called “Neofem2” that affects the mode of social interaction between a queen and workers was discovered in Cryptotermes secundus (Korb et al., 2009b). Under the presence of a queen, workers did not perform head-butting behavior nor differentiate into secondary reproductives. However, when the gene Neofem2 was silenced in the primary queen, workers performed the head-butting behavior and started to reproduce. This result indicated that Neofem2 mediated the reproductive division of labor between queen and workers. Neofem2 encodes β-glycosidase, which was reported as a pheromone involved in egg recognition and communication in termites and cockroaches (Cornette et al., 2003; Matsuura et al., 2009). However, it should be noted that the mechanisms connecting the behavioral regulations and the reproductive differentiation remains to be understood.

In brief, our primary purpose of this review is to summarize the mechanisms of social interactions affecting the regulations of caste differentiation, especially by focusing on the physiological regulations in soldier differentiation. In this article, many studies across various biological processes from the pheromone communications among castes to the alterations of postembryonic development are overviewed, although there are still “missing links” between those processes we here reviewed. For example, the mechanism connecting between social interactions and physiological changes still remains understood. The social physiological mechanisms known in hymenopterans such as the usage of odorant binding proteins (Gp-9) in the fire ant (Gotzek and Ross, 2007) will provide us some hints to complement the missing links. Actually examples of the similar mechanisms related to the social physiology are shared between hymenopterans and termites. In honeybee, vitellogenins are involved in the transition from nursing to foraging in workers (Nelson et al., 2007), while in termites, hexamerins regulate the soldier differentiation (Zhou et al., 2006b; Cornette et al., 2013). Although these two groups of proteins belong to the different families, both are known to be involved in the control of JH titer in insects (Gilbert et al., 2000; Nation, 2008). Therefore, these studies suggest that the sequestration process of JH may be important for the phenotypic transitions such as caste differentiation and age polyethism in social insects. Thus, the in-depth understanding on the complex social interactions in termites will contribute to the deeper understanding of principles in social physiology.

Recently, innovations in a new interdisciplinary science, sociogenomics, and chemical ecology are shedding light on the proximate mechanisms of social interactions regulating caste differentiation, leading to the identifications of candidate factors involved in these mechanisms such as primer pheromones, carrier proteins of pheromones and factors regulating JH titers. Recent advances in genomics, transcriptomics, and bioinformatics are also pushing forward the understanding social physiology. For example, the first termite genome sequencing project has been done in Zootermopsis nevadensis (http://termitegenome.org/). Furthermore, genomics and transciptomics in other termite species are proposed by the two major projects in arthpods: the i5k project (http://arthropodgenomes.org/wiki/i5K; including 25 termite species) and 1KITE project (http://www.1kite.org/index.html; including 4 termite species). The future contributions of these projects, together with the achievements in previous studies (e.g., The Honeybee Genome Sequencing Consortium, 2006; Bonasio et al., 2010), will lead to the comprehensive understandings of insect sociality. For example, comparative genomics may reveal the commonalties and diversities of social physiology seen in various lineages of social insects.

The authors declare that the research was conducted in the absence of any commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.

title: Comprehensive Genomic Analysis Reveals Novel Transposable Element-Derived MicroRNA Regulating Caste Differentiation in Honeybees
abstract: AbstractThe honeybee (Apis mellifera) is a highly social insect whose caste differentiation is regulated by epigenetic mechanisms, representing a classic example of phenotypic plasticity in social insects. Although the importance of transposable elements (TEs) in epigenetic research is well recognized, their specific role in honeybee caste differentiation has not been fully explored. This study reveals a novel regulatory mechanism where the microRNA (miRNA) ame-mir-3721-3p, derived from ApME (Apis miniature inverted-repeat TEs), suppresses DNA methyltransferase gene DNMT3, promoting queen-like development in honeybee larvae. Genome-wide analysis identified 43 ApME elements in Apis, with ApMETm15 being particularly abundant and species-specific. These elements gave rise to 6 miRNAs, including ame-mir-3721-3p which showed notable regulatory potential. Target gene prediction and luciferase reporter assays confirmed that ame-mir-3721-3p binds to and suppresses DNMT3 expression. Spatiotemporal expression analysis indicated that ame-mir-3721-3p is significantly upregulated during the critical L3 larval stage, exhibiting a similar expression pattern to DNMT3. Larval feeding experiments with agomir demonstrated that ame-mir-3721-3p suppresses DNMT3 expression and significantly impacts the expression of genes related to the juvenile hormone and ecdysone pathways. Further physiological evidence showed that when larvae were treated with agomir-3721 during the critical caste differentiation window (L3-L4 stage), the emerging adult bees exhibited increased body size, doubled ovarian area, and significantly higher frequency of ovary development, with significant upregulation of ovarian-specific marker genes. These findings provide direct evidence for ame-mir-3721-3p's role in promoting queen-like developmental trajectories during caste differentiation, uncovering a new regulatory pathway in honeybee development and offering insights into epigenetic mechanisms in social insects.
body_text:
The honeybee (Apis mellifera) exemplifies the complexity of social insect organization, functioning as a “superorganism” through sophisticated division of labor, resource management, and colony cohesion. Within a typical hive, a single fertile queen coexists with thousands of nonreproductive female workers and varying numbers of haploid drones (Leonhardt et al. 2016, Avalos et al. 2017). Despite sharing identical genomes, queens and workers exhibit striking dimorphism in their reproductive capacity: queens possess fully developed ovaries and maintain reproductive dominance, while workers retain only vestigial ovarian structures. This reproductive divergence extends to broader phenotypic differences, encompassing morphology, behavior, physiology, and longevity (Wheeler 1986). Queens, adapted for their reproductive role, display enhanced size and longevity, while workers exhibit specialized adaptations for diverse colony maintenance tasks. The honeybee's unique caste system and lifespan differentiation make it a powerful model for studying the interplay between aging, development, and social organization (Page and Peng 2001).

This remarkable phenotypic plasticity stems from a sophisticated interplay of environmental factors and regulatory mechanisms during development. The nutritional pathway serves as a primary environmental trigger, with royal jelly exclusively provisioned to queen larvae creating a distinct developmental trajectory through its rich complement of proteins, lipids, and regulatory factors; in contrast, worker development follows an alternative path shaped by a diet of honey and pollen (Evans and Wheeler 2001). This nutritional dichotomy initiates cascade effects through multiple regulatory layers, including hormonal signaling and gene expression networks. For instance, vitellogenin (Vg) expression in queen brain tissue exemplifies the complex interaction between nutrition and developmental regulation (Zhang et al. 2022). The regulatory landscape extends to epigenetic mechanisms, particularly DNA methylation mediated by DNA methyltransferase 3 (DNMT3), which establishes distinct methylation profiles in queen and worker brains (Lyko et al. 2010). DNA methylation marks play crucial roles in regulating gene expression and developmental plasticity in social insects (Li-Byarlay 2016, Wedd et al. 2016). Beyond the canonical roles of DNA methylation, recent studies in mammals have revealed noncanonical DNA methylation variations that significantly expand our understanding of epigenetic regulation (Schultz et al. 2015). These epigenetic patterns respond to and influence social interactions, creating a dynamic regulatory network that shapes caste-specific development (Cardoso-Júnior et al. 2018).

Notably, honeybee caste determination involves a critical developmental time window. Female larvae maintain developmental plasticity (bipotency) until the third larval instar (L3), during which they can develop into either queens or workers (Weaver 1957; Shuel and Dixon 1960). During this period, all larvae receive royal jelly from nurse bees. Subsequently, nurse bees adopt a selective feeding strategy: queen-destined larvae continue to receive abundant royal jelly throughout development, resulting in elevated sugar levels, while worker-destined larvae are switched to restricted amounts of worker jelly after day 3 (Rembold et al. 1980; Kaftanoglu et al. 2011). This differential feeding regime critically influences larval development trajectory and ultimate caste fate (Haydak 1970; Kaftanoglu et al. 2010).

Transposable elements (TEs) represent a fundamental component of eukaryotic genomes, significantly influencing genomic organization and evolution. First discovered in maize (McClintock 1950), TEs were shown to have the ability to move within the genome, creating mutations and altering gene expression (Kidwell and Lisch 2001). These mobile genetic elements are classified into 2 major categories: class I retrotransposons, which transpose via RNA intermediates, and class II DNA transposons, which move directly as DNA segments (Rebollo et al. 2012). Among class II elements, miniature inverted-repeat TEs (MITEs) have attracted particular attention due to their distinctive characteristics and widespread distribution. First identified in maize as the Tourist element, MITEs are characterized by their small size, high copy numbers, and conserved terminal inverted repeats (TIRs) flanked by target site duplications (Bureau and Wessler 1992).

Although MITEs lack autonomous transposition capability, their mobility depends on transposases provided by autonomous elements, suggesting their origin through internal deletions of autonomous DNA transposons (Casacuberta and Santiago 2003, Feschotte and Pritham 2007). This relationship was demonstrated through studies of the mPing element in Arabidopsis thaliana, where autonomous transposons undergo a specific deletion process: they lose their internal transposase-coding sequences while maintaining their TIRs. These resulting shortened elements become MITEs, which, despite losing their ability to produce transposase, can still be mobilized by transposases produced by their intact parent elements (Yang et al. 2007). Recent investigations in insects, particularly in lepidopteran genomes, have revealed the extensive distribution and potential regulatory roles of these nonautonomous elements across different species (Klai et al. 2022).

The regulatory complexity of genomic elements is further exemplified by microRNAs (miRNAs), small noncoding RNAs approximately 22 nucleotides in length that function as precise posttranscriptional regulators. These molecules achieve regulatory control through specific interactions with 3′ untranslated regions (3′UTRs) of target messenger RNAs, modulating gene expression through translation inhibition or transcript degradation (Klenov and Gvozdev 2005). In honeybees, RNA pathways have been shown to play critical roles in gene regulation, with evidence suggesting that RNA molecules can be transmitted between individuals, potentially influencing colony-wide gene expression (Maori et al. 2019). Their regulatory influence extends across fundamental biological processes, from cellular differentiation to complex developmental programs (Belles et al. 2012).

Research on transposons in honeybees encompasses their diversity, evolutionary impact, mobilization mechanisms, and regulatory roles, revealing complex patterns in genomic architecture and evolution. Studies of piggyBac transposons within the Apoidea superfamily have demonstrated their crucial role in shaping honeybee genomics (Li et al. 2023), while advances in transposase technology have enabled enhanced genetic transformation methods in honeybees (Otte et al. 2018). The evolutionary dynamics of transposons are further illustrated by the distinctive patterns of pogo and Tc1/mariner elements across bee lineages (Liu et al. 2021). Despite these advances, the functions of MITEs in honeybee evolution, development, and epigenetic regulation remain largely unexplored.

The relationship between TEs and gene regulation has emerged as a critical area of research, particularly through the lens of TE-derived miRNAs. These regulatory molecules have been extensively documented in both plant and animal systems, demonstrating their fundamental role in posttranscriptional regulation. In plants, MITEs have been particularly significant in the evolution of miRNA genes, creating novel regulatory networks that enhance environmental adaptability (Pegler et al. 2023). This adaptive potential is reflected in their strategic positioning within or near genes, facilitating the integration of new regulatory mechanisms.

The regulatory significance of TE-derived miRNAs extends into animal systems, where they exhibit remarkable evolutionary conservation and functional diversity. These elements have been shown to modulate gene expression networks across various species (Mustafin and Khusnutdinova 2023), with human studies revealing sophisticated targeting mechanisms for specific mRNA regions (Qin et al. 2015). The evolutionary conservation of these regulatory mechanisms underscores their fundamental importance in genetic regulation.

The broader context of TE-derived regulatory elements includes complex interactions within regulatory networks, particularly evident in the diverse roles of small RNAs. This is exemplified in studies of Anopheles gambiae, where TEs contribute substantially to siRNA and piRNA populations, comprising 56% to 60% of these regulatory molecules in adult females (Biryukova and Ye 2015). These findings align with broader observations about the evolutionary significance of TE-derived miRNAs in gene expression control across animal species (Gebrie 2023).

Building on this foundation, our study presents the first comprehensive analysis of MITEs in the genus Apis and their derived miRNAs (ApME-miRNAs). We specifically focused on a miRNA derived from the ApMETm15 element, ame-mir-3721-3p, specific to the honeybee (A. mellifera). Through systematic target gene prediction and experimental validation, we established that ame-mir-3721-3p functions as a regulatory molecule for DNMT3, thereby influencing the critical process of caste differentiation in honeybees.

Using MITE-Hunter, along with subsequent screening and alignment, we identified 43 Apis MITEs (abbreviated as ApME, also expressed in this manner below). ApME origins can be categorized into three types: piggyBac transposons, Tc1/mariner transposons, and those of unknown origins (supplementary table S1, Supplementary Materail online). Most ApME originated from Tc1/mariner transposons, accounting for 22 elements (51.2%). There are 11 ApME of unknown origin (25.6%), and 10 ApME originated from piggyBac transposons (23.3%) (Fig. 1a). Overall, ApME is mainly derived from transposase-deficient Tc1/mariner and piggyBac transposons.

Identification, distribution, and genomic features of ApME (Apis MITEs) in Apis species. a) Distribution of ApME based on their origins, classified into piggyBac-originated (ApMEPb), Tc1/mariner-originated (ApMETm), and unknown origin (ApMEUn). b) ApME copy number variations across different Apis genomes. c) Copy number variations of ApME in 5 Apis genomes, with asterisks and boxes highlighting ApME unique to specific Apis species. The scale bar on the right side of the figure represents the corresponding length of 100 copies. d) Kimura distance-based analysis of insertion burst timings of ApME TEs. The x axis shows the Kimura substitution level (pairwise distance), which serves as a molecular clock indicating the relative age of transposon insertions—smaller values represent more recent insertion events while larger values indicate older insertion events. The y axis shows the density of transposon copies at each substitution level, reflecting the intensity of transposition activity at different time points. e) Comparative genomic distribution of ApME insertions across chromosomes in different Apis species. a) Reference chromosomes of Apis (Chr1-16); b) ApME distribution in A. cerana Hainan genome; c) ApME distribution in A. cerana Aba genome; d) ApME distribution in A. mellifera genome. Different colors indicate species-specific and shared ApME insertions. f) Distribution of ApME insertion frequencies across different genomic features: 3′UTR, 5′UTR, CDS (coding sequences), exon, gene body (from transcription start to end), and gene-proximal regions (comprising 5,000 bp upstream of transcription start site and 5,000 bp downstream of transcription end site). The y axis represents the relative density of insertions normalized to the total number of insertion sites.

By aligning ApME sequences to the genomes of various Apis species, we discovered significant differences in the copy numbers of these transposons, indicating species-specific ApME characteristics. Apis laboriosa and Apis dorsata exhibited higher ApME copy numbers (958 and 821 copies, respectively). However, these numbers should be interpreted with caution since both genomes are currently assembled at the scaffold level rather than chromosome level, which may lead to overestimation of repetitive element copy numbers due to potential assembly artifacts and incomplete sequence consolidation. Unlike chromosome-level assemblies where repetitive sequences are more accurately placed and merged, scaffold-level assemblies may contain redundant copies of the same elements across different scaffolds. Apis mellifera and Apis florea had intermediate copy numbers (763 and 709 copies, respectively), while Apis cerana had the fewest copies of 459 (Fig. 1b). At comparable genome assembly levels, A. mellifera showed significantly more ApME copies than A. cerana. This difference was primarily due to the high copy numbers of 3 ApME elements specific to A. mellifera: ApMETm14, ApMETm15, and ApMEPb4 (Fig. 1c). Notably, ApMETm15, with 249 copies, was the most abundant ApME in A. mellifera, indicating its important biological role in this species. Additionally, ApMEPb1 was unique to A. cerana, ApMEPb3 to A. laboriosa, and ApMEPb6 and ApMEPb9 to A. florea. We also compared ApME copy numbers among various subspecies of A. cerana (supplementary fig. S1, Supplementary Material online).

Due to significant differences in length and sequence among ApME elements, constructing a highly confident phylogenetic tree was not feasible. Therefore, we conducted clustering analysis based on sequence similarity scores (supplementary fig. S4, Supplementary Material online). The results showed that most ApME elements originating from Tc1/mariner transposons had high similarity scores and clustered together, consistent with the origin analysis results. To explore the insertion burst timing of different ApME elements, we performed analysis based on Kimura distance, which indicated that most ApME elements had similar insertion times (supplementary fig. S2, Supplementary Material online). Notably, ApMETm15 and ApMETm5 show the oldest insertion mutation peaks (Fig. 1d). This represents a greater accumulation of mutations between their copies, suggesting that ApMETm15 and ApMETm5 may have been inserted into the bee genome earlier in ApME.

We mapped the precise insertion sites of ApME in the genomes of both A. cerana and A. mellifera (Fig. 1e). The results showed that except for the A. mellifera–specific ApMETm14 and ApMETm15 with high copy numbers, other common ApME elements exhibited similar insertion patterns, preferring the ends of chromosomes in both species. The A. mellifera–specific ApME significantly contributed to the genomic differences between the 2 species. Additionally, ApME elements were predominantly found inserted into specific genomic regions, predominantly within 5,000 bp upstream and downstream of genes and within gene bodies, while insertions in other UTR, CDS, and exon regions were less frequent (Fig. 1f). This suggests that ApME may play important roles in regulating gene expression and influencing genome structural stability.

MITEs have emerged as important contributors to the miRNA pool in various organisms. In this study, we undertook a comprehensive identification and prediction process for miRNAs derived from ApME elements. Using a combination of alignment and screening techniques, we identified 6 ApME-miRNAs (ApME-derived miRNAs): ame-mir-9895-3p, ame-mir-6004-5p, ame-mir-3716-3p, and ame-mir-9886-3p from ApMETm14; ame-mir-3721-3p from ApMETm15; and ame-mir-9872-5p from ApMETm3, ApMETm5, and ApMETm16 (Fig. 2a). Notably, ApMETm14 and ApMETm15 represent A. mellifera–specific TEs with high copy numbers, while ApMETm16, ApMETm3, and ApMETm5 share high sequence similarity. These mapping patterns may influence various biological phenomena in A. mellifera, which requires further experimental validation. To delve deeper into their functional potential, we predicted the secondary structures of these miRNAs using RNAfold. The analysis revealed stable secondary structures for all 6 miRNAs (Fig. 2b). The mfe values, typically ranging from 0.1 to 0.9 with most stable regions showing values above 0.7, were indicative of the energy required to maintain these structures. Additionally, we used probability density function (pf) and centroid predictions to assess the structural variability, which showed entropy values generally ranging between 15 and 30, suggesting these miRNAs are structurally conserved and stable. All 6 miRNAs demonstrated characteristic stem-loop structures with stem lengths of 30 to 45 nucleotides, further supporting their identity as genuine miRNAs.

Identification and structural characterization of ApME-derived miRNAs in A. mellifera. a) Several ApME-miRNAs derived from different ApMEs were identified in this study. The first column of the table lists the ApME sources, while the second column shows their corresponding ApME-miRNAs. Notably, ApMETm15 is marked with a red star, indicating that its associated miRNA (ame-mir-3721-3p) is a key candidate for further investigation. b) Secondary structure predictions of 6 ApME-derived miRNAs using RNAfold. For each miRNA, 3 parameters are shown: minimum free energy structure (mfe), partition function folding (pf), and centroid structure. The color gradients in the structures represent base-pair probabilities (red: high probability; blue: low probability). Position-wise entropy values are plotted below each structure. The y axis shows the height (0 to 1.0) of base-pair probability, and the x axis represents nucleotide positions.

These findings not only validate our computational predictions but also highlight the potential regulatory roles of these ApME-derived miRNAs in honeybee biology. The structural stability and conservation of these miRNAs suggest that they could be integral components in gene regulatory networks, potentially influencing various biological processes.

To explore the gene regulatory roles of ApME-derived miRNAs (ApME-miRNAs), we employed 3 prediction tools to identify their target genes and conducted intersection screening. The results showed variability in the number of predicted target genes, with ame-mir-9895 having the highest number and ame-mir-3716 the fewest. Ame-mir-3721-3p had 875 predicted target genes (Fig. 3a). To pinpoint the most significant target genes, we performed hub gene prediction and displayed the top 10 genes with the highest central network scores (Fig. 3b). “Darker colors represent higher scores, indicating stronger predicted targeting relationships between ApME-miRNAs and their potential regulatory targets, thus suggesting promising candidates for experimental validation. Among these, we particularly focused on ame-mir-3721-3p, derived from the A. mellifera–specific and highly duplicated ApMETm15, which targets DNMT3, a key regulator of DNA methylation and caste differentiation (supplementary fig. S3, Supplementary Material online). This regulatory relationship warranted further investigation due to its potential significance in honeybee development.

Target gene and hub gene prediction of ApME-miRNAs and their KEGG pathway analysis. a) Quantitative distribution of predicted target genes for 6 ApME-miRNAs, with ame-mir-9886-3p showing the highest number of target genes (3,312, 42.272%), followed by ame-mir-9872-5p (2,120, 27.058%), and other miRNAs ranging from 411 to 875 target genes. b) Network analysis of hub genes targeted by ApME-miRNAs. The heat map displays key hub genes for each miRNA, including important regulatory genes such as DNMT3, Foxp, and various neurotransmitter receptors (e.g. DopR2, 5-HT2β). The intensity of color represents the centrality score of each gene within the network, with darker colors indicating higher network importance. c) KEGG pathway enrichment analysis for target genes of each ApME-miRNA, presented as bubble plots. The size of each bubble represents the count of genes involved in the pathway, while the color intensity indicates the adjusted P-value significance level. Pathways marked in blue (Hippo signaling pathway, MAPK signaling pathway, Wnt signaling pathway) are widely present in the target genes of the 6 ApME-miRNAs.

To understand the biological pathways modulated by ApME-derived miRNAs, we conducted KEGG pathway analysis on their predicted target genes. The target genes of ame-mir-3721-3p were notably enriched in the Hippo signaling pathway, a common enrichment seen in other ApME-miRNAs as well. The Hippo pathway is vital for regulating organ size, tissue homeostasis, and cell proliferation, playing pivotal roles in development, regeneration, and cancer. Additionally, the Wnt signaling pathway, crucial for embryonic development, tissue homeostasis, cell proliferation, differentiation, and stem cell maintenance, was significantly enriched. The MAPK signaling pathway, a conserved pathway regulating proliferation, differentiation, survival, and apoptosis, also showed notable enrichment (Fig. 3c). These findings suggest that ApME-miRNAs are integral in regulating key developmental and proliferative pathways.

Given the predicted importance of ame-mir-3721-3p, particularly due to its derivation from the highly abundant ApMETm15 element, we performed PCR and sequencing validations to confirm its existence. The PCR results displayed a clear single band, which indicates a specific amplification of ame-mir-3721-3p without any nonspecific products (supplementary fig. S5a, Supplementary Material online). Subsequent sequencing of the PCR product matched the predicted sequence perfectly, confirming the presence and accuracy of our miRNA prediction (supplementary fig. S5b, Supplementary Material online).

We measured the expression levels of ame-mir-3721-3p and DNMT3 in honeybee larvae at different ages. Queen larvae (Q) and worker larvae (W) showed distinct patterns of ame-mir-3721-3p expression (Fig. 4a). Notably, ame-mir-3721-3p expression was significantly higher in queen larvae on the third day compared to other ages and worker larvae, indicating its potential importance and specific expression pattern during early honeybee development. Queens show significantly lower DNMT3 expression than worker larvae in the third instar (Fig. 4b). Representative photographs document the L3 and L4 larval stages (Fig. 4c), corresponding to the developmental period when ame-mir-3721-3p and DNMT3 expression changes were analyzed. During the third larval day, ame-mir-3721-3p and DNMT3 displayed inverse expression patterns in queen larvae, with high levels of ame-mir-3721-3p corresponding to low DNMT3 expression, suggesting a potential suppressive regulatory relationship between this miRNA and its target gene. Since DNMT3 is a DNA methyltransferase involved in the DNA methylation process in honeybees, changes in its expression could affect gene expression and cell function, leading to developmental differences between queen and worker larvae. The specific regulation of DNMT3 expression by ame-mir-3721-3p may represent an important molecular mechanism in the age-dependent development of honeybee larvae.

Spatiotemporal expression of ame-mir-3721-3p and DNMT3 in honeybee Larvae and their effects on JH and Ecr pathways. a) Spatiotemporal expression profiles of ame-mir-3721-3p in queen (QL) and worker larvae (WL) during L2, L3, and L4 stages. b) Spatiotemporal expression profiles of DNMT3 in queen and worker larvae during L2, L3, and L4 stages. c) Microscopic images of queen and worker larvae on day 2 and day 3. d) Luciferase reporter assay demonstrating the inhibitory binding of ame-mir-3721-3p to the DNMT3 3′UTR. e) Differential expression analysis of DNMT3 from 6 to 24 h after feeding L2 larvae with agomir-NC and agomir-3721. f) Impact of agomir-3721 feeding on juvenile hormone pathway genes (JHAMT, Vg). g) Impact of agomir-3721 feeding on ecdysone receptor pathway genes (EcrA, EcrB).

To validate the interaction between ame-mir-3721-3p and the DNMT3 3′UTR, we performed dual-luciferase reporter assays. The reporter constructs contained the DNMT3 3′UTR sequence downstream of the luciferase gene, with Renilla luciferase serving as an internal control. Transfection with 20 pmol of synthetic ame-mir-3721-3p mimics resulted in a significant reduction in the normalized luciferase/Renilla (Luc/REN) ratio compared to negative controls (NC) (Fig. 4d). This decrease in reporter activity demonstrates specific binding of ame-mir-3721-3p to the DNMT3 3′UTR sequence, confirming the direct regulation of DNMT3 by this miRNA.

The juvenile hormone (JH) pathway and ecdysone receptor (Ecr) pathway are crucial for the development and caste differentiation of honeybee larvae (Robinson and Vargo 1997). This study demonstrated the effective binding of ame-mir-3721-3p to the DNMT3 and suggesting its potential role as a major participant in the regulatory network influencing caste differentiation, as evidenced by in vitro feeding experiments. We synthesized a miRNA mimic for ame-mir-3721-3p (agomir) and its negative control (agomir-NC) and fed them to 1-day-old A. mellifera larvae through an artificial diet. DNMT3 expression was significantly suppressed 6 h after feeding with agomir (Fig. 4e). At 12 and 18 h postfeeding, DNMT3 expression levels in the experimental group gradually increased. This increase might be due to a compensatory regulation mechanism in the larvae to maintain normal development. We further examined genes related to the juvenile hormone (JH) pathway and the ecdysone receptor (Ecr) pathway. Six hours after agomir feeding, the expression of the JH pathway-related gene vitellogenin (Vg) was significantly upregulated, while JHAMT expression was significantly suppressed (Fig. 4e). In the Ecr pathway, the expression of EcrA and EcrB genes was significantly inhibited (Fig. 4f). These findings indicate that ame-mir-3721-3p significantly impacts key hormonal pathways involved in honeybee development and caste differentiation, highlighting its essential regulatory functions.

The phenotypic effects of ame-mir-3721-3p on A. mellifera caste differentiation and development were investigated through controlled laboratory rearing experiments. Larvae were divided into agomir-NC control (n = 176) and −3,721 treatment groups (n = 108). The agomir-supplemented diet was administered exclusively before the L3 stage (day 3), followed by standard feeding until pupation. The pupae were maintained in an incubator until emergence, at which point morphological measurements and dissections were performed (supplementary fig. S6b and S6c, Supplementary Material online).

The emergence rates were comparable between groups (61.63% for agomir-NC and 65.96% for agomir-3721-treated larvae; supplementary table S3, Supplementary Material online). Under standardized feeding conditions (controlled food quantity and feeding frequency), bees treated with agomir-3721 up to the third instar larval stage (L3, a critical stage for caste differentiation) showed significantly higher body weights at emergence (0.0906 ± 0.0072 g) compared to the agomir-NC group (0.0862 ± 0.0051 g) (Fig. 5c; supplementary table S3, Supplementary Material online), suggesting that ame-mir-3721-3p intervention during L3 positively influences adult bee weight.

ame-mir-3721-3p promotes queen-like traits and enhances ovarian development in A. mellifera. a) Percentage of bees with developed ovaries in agomir-NC (45.3%) and agomir-3721 (61.3%) groups, showing a significant 16% increase in the agomir-3721 group. b) Quantification of ovarian area (mm²) showing significantly larger ovaries in agomir-3721-treated bees compared to agomir-NC controls (**). c) Body weight comparison of newly emerged bees between agomir-NC and agomir-3721 groups. d) Representative images showing ovarian development in virgin queens, agomir-3721-treated bees, and agomir-NC controls. Scale bars = 1 mm. The agomir-3721-treated ovaries show development approaching that of virgin queens and superior to agomir-NC controls. e) Relative expression of Vg (vitellogenin) normalized to CALM, showing an upward trend in agomir-3721-treated bees (P = 0.0893). f) Relative expression of VgR (vitellogenin receptor) normalized to CALM, demonstrating significantly higher expression in agomir-3721-treated bees (***).

Based on morphological characteristics and the presence of spermatheca (a queen-specific organ), emerged bees were classified as either queen-like (larger body size, elongated abdomen, presence of spermatheca) or worker phenotype (smaller body size, shorter abdomen, absence of spermatheca) (supplementary fig. S6a, Supplementary Material online). The agomir-3721 group showed a modestly higher proportion of queen-like individuals (29.03%) compared to the agomir-NC group (24.52%) (supplementary fig. S6d, Supplementary Material online).

Given that ovarian development is the primary determinant of queen–worker dimorphism (Wheeler 1986), we conducted detailed ovarian dissections. All queen-like individuals exhibited developed ovaries. Among bees that developed into workers, both experimental and control groups contained individuals with either developed or undeveloped ovaries. Notably, the proportion of workers with developed ovaries was significantly higher in the agomir-3721 group (45.5%) compared to the agomir-NC group (27.5%), representing an 18% increase in ovarian development frequency (supplementary fig. S6e, Supplementary Material online). Overall, among all emerged bees examined, the proportion of individuals with developed ovaries was 61.3% in the agomir-3721 group compared to 45.3% in the agomir-NC group, showing a 16% increase (Fig. 5a). These results demonstrate that ame-mir-3721-3p overexpression treatment before L3 significantly enhances ovarian development in emerged adult bees, the defining reproductive trait that differentiates queens from workers.

To further characterize the extent of reproductive development, we performed detailed morphometric analyses of ovarian structures. Ovaries from the agomir-3721 group exhibited significantly larger dimensions across all measured parameters compared to the agomir-NC group. The maximum length increased from 3.18 ± 0.22 mm to 3.82 ± 0.43 mm, and the maximum width expanded from 1.10 ± 0.17 mm to 1.63 ± 0.31 mm in agomir-3721-treated bees. Additionally, microscopic measurements revealed that the total ovarian area in the agomir-3721 group (4.62 ± 0.99 mm²) was more than twice that of the control group (2.25 ± 0.46 mm²) (Fig. 5b; supplementary table S3, Supplementary Material online). Representative microscopy images show that the most developed ovary in the agomir-3721 group approached the development level of naturally reared virgin queen ovaries and was notably more developed than those in the agomir-NC group (Fig. 5d). It should be noted that achieving full queen-level ovarian development under laboratory conditions with royal jelly feeding alone (without gene silencing or other dietary supplements) is challenging due to various limitations, including suboptimal artificial royal jelly nutrition, lack of appropriate-sized natural cells, potential mechanical damage during artificial feeding, and absence of worker bee care behaviors. Despite these constraints, these substantial increases in ovarian dimensions indicate that ame-mir-3721-3p not only promotes the frequency of ovarian development but also enhances the degree of development.

Based on the previous morphological observations, we further examined the expression levels of key genes closely related to reproductive development. In newly emerged agomir-3721 and agomir-NC-treated bees, we analyzed the expression of vitellogenin receptor (VgR) and vitellogenin (Vg). VgR is a transmembrane receptor specifically expressed in ovarian tissue, mediating vitellogenin transport from hemolymph to developing oocytes (Cardoso-Júnior et al. 2021). Due to its tissue-specific expression pattern, VgR expression level is considered a reliable indicator of ovarian developmental status. Results showed that VgR expression was significantly higher in the agomir-3721 group compared to the control (Fig. 5f). Vg, as the major yolk protein precursor, is primarily synthesized in the fat body and secreted into the hemolymph, subsequently being taken up by oocytes through binding to VgR (Corona et al. 2007). Although Vg expression in the agomir-3721 group did not reach statistical significance (P = 0.0893), it showed an upward trend (Fig. 5e). Given the ovary-specific expression of VgR and its crucial role in oocyte development, its expression level serves as a more direct indicator of ovarian development status (Cardoso-Júnior et al. 2021). The significant upregulation of VgR and the upward trend of Vg corroborate our previous morphological observations.

Our study elucidates the molecular mechanism by which ame-mir-3721-3p, derived from the TE ApMETm15, regulates the DNA methyltransferase DNMT3 during the L3 larval stage, a critical developmental window for honeybee (A. mellifera) caste differentiation, and presents a proposed model for its potential regulatory mechanisms (Fig. 6). This work not only underscores the specific impact of ame-mir-3721-3p on caste differentiation but also sheds light on the broader role of TEs in gene regulatory networks and their potential implications for biological evolution and epigenetic regulation in social insects.

A proposed model for the endogenous molecular mechanism of ApMETm15-derived ame-mir-3721-3p in caste differentiation of A. mellifera. In nature, during early larval development (L1 stage), all honeybee larvae receive royal jelly feeding, yet some develop into queens while others become workers. A critical window period exists at the L3 stage, where caste fate becomes determined-even continued royal jelly feeding after this stage cannot alter the developmental trajectory. One of the most significant differences between queens and workers is their ovarian development, with queens possessing fully functional reproductive ovaries while workers have underdeveloped, nonreproductive ones. Our study reveals that ApMETm15, a MITE unique to A. mellifera, serves as the genomic source of ame-mir-3721-3p. ame-mir-3721-3p suppresses DNMT3 expression by binding to its 3′UTR region. This suppression positions DNMT3 as a potential key regulator of downstream hormonal pathways, influencing critical genes in the juvenile hormone pathway (Vg, JHAMT) and ecdysone receptor pathway genes (EcrA, EcrB). This molecular mechanism, operating during the critical window period of caste differentiation, represents an endogenous regulatory pathway that influences caste differentiation biological phenotypes, particularly in determining reproductive capacity through ovarian development patterns that distinguish queens from workers.

Since the 1950s, the mechanism behind queen and worker differentiation in honeybees has been a topic of great interest (Weaver 1957, Weaver 1966, Rembold et al. 1980). Early studies showed that worker larvae are totipotent within the first 3 days after hatching. If transferred to a queen cell and nurtured in the hive, they can still develop into nearly normal queens. After 3.5 d of age, the developmental trajectory becomes fixed, and the worker larvae can only develop into workers regardless of their subsequent feeding regime. The period from 3 to 3.5 d posthatching, known as the L3-L3.5 stage, is thus a critical window for caste differentiation in honeybees. Most studies on honeybee caste differentiation focus on the fourth day after larval hatching, as many caste-related genes peak in expression at this time, showcasing significant physiological and gene expression changes (Barchuk et al. 2007, Shi et al. 2015, Wang et al. 2020). However, this focus may overlook some early gene regulatory mechanisms that occur prior to caste differentiation.

Our data indicate that the expression of ame-mir-3721-3p significantly increases on the third day posthatching, correlating closely with the spatiotemporal expression pattern of DNMT3. DNMT3 has been extensively studied in honeybees and is considered a key epigenetic regulator in caste differentiation, affecting developmental pathways of queens and workers through genome-wide methylation regulation (Lyko et al. 2010). RNA interference knockdown of DNMT3 has been shown to alter alternative splicing events in honeybee genes, further underscoring its essential role in development and gene regulation (Li-Byarlay et al. 2013).
