This suggests a possible synergistic regulatory relationship between ame-mir-3721-3p and DNMT3 during the critical window of caste differentiation. Further target gene predictions and luciferase reporter assays confirm that ame-mir-3721 specifically binds to the 3′UTR of DNMT3 mRNA, significantly inhibiting its expression. Related studies show that dsRNA-mediated DNMT3 knockdown in larvae leads to queen-like physiological characteristics, including increased body size and accelerated ovary development (Kucharski et al. 2008).

We further investigated the impact of ame-mir-3721-3p on downstream developmental genes by constructing agomir-3721, a mimic that enhances ame-mir-3721-3p expression, and performing in vitro feeding experiments on larvae. The results showed that the significant inhibition of DNMT3 expression was accompanied by a marked upregulation of the juvenile hormone pathway gene Vg and a pronounced downregulation of the ecdysone pathway genes EcrA and EcrB. These findings highlight DNMT3 as a potential key mediator of these changes, likely functioning within a broader regulatory network modulated by ame-mir-3721-3p. Vitellogenin (Vg) and ecdysone receptor (EcR) play critical roles in caste differentiation in honeybee larvae. Studies have shown that high Vg expression serves as a “molecular signature” for queen development (Zhang et al. 2022), while low EcR expression, combined with reduced ecdysone levels, supports the queen developmental pathway. In contrast, worker larvae exhibit high EcR expression and enhanced ecdysone signaling, which promote the specialization of somatic tissues (Mello et al. 2014). Our findings are consistent with previous studies. Interestingly, we found that JHAMT expression was significantly downregulated following agomir-3721 feeding. While this might initially appear counterintuitive, previous studies have revealed that JHAMT expression patterns during caste differentiation do not follow a simple correlation with queen development. Studies of JHAMT expression in the A. mellifera corpora allata have demonstrated that worker larvae actually maintain higher JHAMT transcript levels than queen larvae during the L4 stage (Bomtorin et al. 2014). This differential expression pattern has also been independently confirmed in whole-body analyses, where JHAMT expression was also found to be elevated in worker larvae compared to queen larvae during this critical developmental period (Li et al. 2013). Our observed downregulation of JHAMT following agomir-3721 treatment is therefore consistent with these established expression patterns, suggesting that JHAMT regulation during caste differentiation is more complex than initially assumed and does not simply mirror JH titers or queen developmental trajectory. In summary, our study reveals that ame-mir-3721-3p regulates DNMT3 expression, and accompanied by changes in the expression of juvenile hormone and ecdysone pathway genes, that control caste differentiation.

In mammals, DNA methylation typically represses gene expression by modifying promoter regions, blocking transcription factor binding and RNA polymerase recruitment (Lo and Weksberg 2014). In insects, however, DNA methylation predominantly occurs within gene body regions (intragenic regions) and is more strongly associated with alternative splicing or transcriptional stability rather than direct transcriptional repression (Feng et al. 2010; Lyko et al. 2010). As such, the relationship between DNA methylation and gene expression in insects is weaker and more variable compared to mammals. Our findings indicate that DNMT3 is likely involved in regulating downstream gene expression during caste differentiation. However, the precise mechanism by which DNMT3 influences gene expression remains unclear. One possibility is that DNMT3-mediated DNA methylation indirectly affects transcriptional efficiency or alternative splicing, consistent with previous studies in insects (Lyko et al. 2010; Glastad et al. 2011). Another possibility is that DNMT3 operates as part of a broader regulatory network modulated by ame-mir-3721-3p. While DNMT3 was identified as a direct target of ame-mir-3721-3p, it cannot be ruled out that other, unexamined targets of ame-mir-3721-3p contribute to the observed changes by acting as upstream regulators. These upstream factors may influence the expression of genes involved in hormonal signaling pathways, such as juvenile hormone and ecdysone pathways, which are critical for caste differentiation. Future research will focus on elucidating the specific molecular mechanisms linking DNMT3 activity to downstream gene regulation. This includes investigating whether DNMT3-mediated DNA methylation affects transcriptional efficiency or alternative splicing, as well as identifying other potential targets of ame-mir-3721-3p that may function as key regulators in hormonal signaling pathways. Such studies will provide deeper insights into the complex regulatory networks underlying caste differentiation in honeybees.

Based on these molecular findings, we next sought to provide direct physiological evidence for the role of ame-mir-3721-3p in caste determination by rearing honeybee larvae to adult emergence under laboratory conditions. Through comprehensive physiological experiments, we systematically demonstrated that ame-mir-3721-3p promotes developmental bias toward queen-like traits during honeybee caste differentiation. Under controlled laboratory conditions, larvae receiving agomir-3721 treatment exhibited comparable emergence rates to controls (65.96% vs. 61.63%), indicating that the treatment did not impair normal development. Notably, these treated bees showed a developmental tendency toward queen-like characteristics, as evidenced by significantly increased body weights (0.0906 ± 0.0072 g vs. 0.0862 ± 0.0051 g in controls) and a higher proportion showing queen-like external morphology, specifically larger body size and elongated abdomen (29.03% vs. 24.52%).

Ovarian development represents the primary determinant of queen–worker dimorphism in honeybees, serving as the most reliable indicator of reproductive potential and caste differentiation (Winston 1991; Hartfelder and Engels 1998). Given this central role, we conducted detailed analyses of ovarian development, which revealed that ame-mir-3721-3p enhanced both the frequency and degree of ovarian development. Among all emerged bees, the proportion of individuals with developed ovaries increased from 45.3% in controls to 61.3% in the treatment group. This developmental bias was particularly evident in worker-type individuals, where the frequency of developed ovaries rose by 18% (45.5% vs. 27.5%). Morphometric measurements further supported this developmental tendency, with treated bees showing significantly enlarged ovarian dimensions—maximum length (3.82 ± 0.43 mm vs. 3.18 ± 0.22 mm), maximum width (1.63 ± 0.31 mm vs. 1.10 ± 0.17 mm), and, most notably, total ovarian area more than doubled (4.62 ± 0.99 mm² vs. 2.25 ± 0.46 mm²). While not reaching the developmental level of hive-reared virgin queens, these enhanced ovaries showed clear progression toward queen-like reproductive characteristics.

At the molecular level, these morphological shifts were accompanied by significant upregulation of VgR, an ovarian-specific marker essential for vitellogenin uptake during oocyte development, with a concurrent upward trend in Vg expression (P = 0.0893). These molecular changes provide a mechanistic basis for the observed developmental bias. Collectively, despite the inherent limitations of laboratory rearing conditions, our multi-level evidence demonstrates that ame-mir-3721-3p functions as a crucial regulator promoting developmental trajectories toward queen-like characteristics during the critical L3 larval stage of honeybee caste differentiation.

Interestingly, in honeybee colonies that have lost their queen and lack the ability to raise a new one, some worker bees develop their ovaries and lay eggs, becoming “laying workers.” This phenomenon has traditionally been attributed to the absence of queen pheromones (Miller and Ratnieks 2001; Hoover et al. 2003). Our findings regarding ame-mir-3721-3p's role in promoting ovarian development through DNMT3 regulation may provide additional molecular insights into this phenomenon. The suppression of DNMT3 expression by ame-mir-3721-3p leads to enhanced ovarian development, similar to the physiological changes observed in laying workers. This suggests that the absence of queen pheromones might trigger changes in epigenetic regulation, potentially including altered expression of ame-mir-3721-3p or related pathways. Previous studies have shown that queen pheromones can influence DNA methylation patterns in worker bees (Grozinger et al. 2007; Herb et al. 2012), and our results suggest a possible mechanistic link between pheromone signaling and epigenetic regulation of reproductive development.

Through comparative genomic analysis within the genus Apis, we identified that ApMETm15 and its derivative, ame-mir-3721-3p, are unique to A. mellifera, suggesting a species-specific evolutionary adaptation. Further analysis of the insertion timing of ApMETm15 indicates it is an ancient event that has persisted in the genome over evolutionary timescales. This long-term retention highlights the potential regulatory roles of TEs, which not only contribute to genome evolution but also act as epigenetic modulators through mechanisms such as DNA methylation and chromatin remodeling, as demonstrated in other systems (Slotkin and Martienssen 2007). From an evolutionary perspective, transposon insertions that are retained in the genome and not deleted often act as enhancers and cis-regulatory elements. These cis-regulatory elements preexist within the TEs and are immediately selected upon insertion or after modifying the surrounding environment. Numerous classic empirical studies have demonstrated how these “ready-made” cis-elements are integrated into the “natural” regulatory apparatus of adjacent genes (Britten 1996, Brosius 2003), including miRNAs (Borchert et al. 2006). This implies that the specific insertion of ApMETm15 into the A. mellifera genome occurred long ago and has persisted, indicating a probable evolutionary advantage and an absence of strong negative selection pressure. Our research indicates that ame-mir-3721-3p targets and suppresses the expression of DNMT3 during the critical larval stage of queen development, thereby promoting queen-specific traits such as ovary development. The downstream gene expression trends in the JH and Ecr pathways further support this finding. Based on this, we hypothesize that the unique insertion of ApMETm15 may provide reproductive advantages to A. mellifera queens.

In conclusion, our study demonstrates that ame-mir-3721-3p, derived from the TE ApMETm15, plays a significant role in honeybee caste differentiation during the critical L3-L3.5 developmental window. This miRNA functions by targeting and suppressing DNMT3, a key epigenetic regulator, thereby influencing DNA methylation patterns crucial for caste determination. The regulatory effects manifest through altered expression of hormone pathway genes and ultimately promote queen-like developmental tendencies, particularly evident in enhanced ovarian development. This molecular mechanism, specifically found in A. mellifera, illustrates how a TE-derived miRNA has become part of the regulatory network governing caste differentiation. Our findings not only reveal a novel regulatory pathway in social insect development but also provide insights into the potential roles of TEs in gene regulatory networks.

To identify candidate MITEs within the Apis genome, we utilized 9 high-quality genomes from the genus Apis, obtained from the NCBI public database. These include the genomes of A. mellifera (GCA_003254395.2), A. dorsata (GCA_000469605.1), A. florea (GCA_000184785.2), A. laboriosa (GCA_014066325.1), A. cerana koreana (GCA_029169275.1), A. cerana wufu (GCA_002290385.1), and A. cerana pakistan (GCA_019250055.1). In addition, we incorporated the genome data of A. cerana abansis (GCA_020141525.2) from our previous research. This comprehensive data set aims to achieve more accurate identification results. We utilized MITE-Hunter (Han and Wessler 2010), which searches for valid TIRs within a specified length range (50 to 800 bp). The parameters for MITE-Hunter were set as follows: TIR length: 5 to 60 bp; target site duplication (TSD) length: 2 to 20 bp; total length: <800 bp; and TIR mismatch: <2. Candidate MITE sequences were manually checked for TIR and TSD characteristics to eliminate sequences incorrectly identified as MITEs due to high copy numbers. We extracted the top 100 BLAST hits for each indeterminate consensus sequence from the genome comparison results and globally aligned them using MUSCLE (Robert et al. 2004). The alignments were then examined in BioEdit, where boundaries were manually defined to confirm TSD and TIR sequences. The corrected MITEs were subsequently processed in DAMBE (Xia 2018) to generate consensus sequences. To ensure accuracy, each species' consensus sequences were compared using BLASTN. If any sequences exhibited more than 80% similarity, the shorter sequence was discarded. The final set of sequences displayed less than 80% similarity to each other. This procedure was repeated for all 9 species to determine accurate MITE consensus sequences, thereby constructing a comprehensive repeat sequence database.

After identifying candidate MITE consensus sequence in Apis, we compared them to the latest Repbase (Kapitonov and Jurka 2008) database (Repbase29.02) using BLASTn. We manually examined the top 50 BLAST hits, and sequences with more than 70% (i.e. 35 or more) matches to the same superfamily were classified under that superfamily. This 70% threshold was established based on empirical testing and follows the unified classification system for TEs (Wicker et al. 2007), as it provides optimal discrimination between superfamilies while maintaining classification accuracy. Sequences that did not meet this criterion were considered unidentified. Based on the superfamily origins of the MITE sequences, we classified and named them as follows: ApMETm (Tc1/mariner originated), ApMEPb (piggyBac originated), and ApMEUn (unknown originated).

In order to estimate the copy number of ApME in various Apis species' genomes, we conducted a BLASTN search with an e-value cutoff of 1e-5, followed by processing of alignment files using SAMtools (Li et al. 2009) for filtering and extracting relevant data.

Sequences showing at least 80% similarity and over 40% coverage were identified as ApME copies. These potential copies were then carefully examined to confirm that they displayed MITE sequence traits, such as complete TIR and TSD sequences.

To further validate and confirm the origins and classifications of the identified ApME sequences, we conducted pairwise comparisons of the high-accuracy ApME consensus sequences using BLASTn. Upon obtaining the sequence similarities, we constructed a similarity matrix and performed clustering analysis. To analyze the expansion of MITE transposon families in different Apis genomes, we aligned all sequences from each family with a similarity of at least 80% and coverage of more than 20% using MUSCLE. Subsequently, we calculated genetic distances using the Kimura-2 parameter model in MEGA7 (Kumar et al. 2016) to represent expansion states. We performed density distribution analysis of genetic distances of different families of ApME using R.

We extracted the positional information of all ApME copies in the genomes of A. mellifera, A. cerana Hainan, and A. cerana Aba using Perl scripts. Using the chromosomes of A. mellifera as reference, we created a fine-scale genomic insertion map with Circos (Krzywinski et al. 2009). To explore the insertion preferences of ApME within the A. mellifera genome and analyze the functions of nearby genes (genes within gene regions and gene flanking regions), we used customized Perl scripts to extract sequences from gene regions, intergenic regions, gene flanking regions (within 5,000 bp), exonic regions, and intronic regions. We then compared representative Tc1/mariner sequences to these extracted sequences using blastn, manually corrected and filtered the results, and recorded the insertion positions.

We downloaded all mature miRNA and miRNA precursor sequences for A. mellifera from miRbase (https://www.mirbase.org). Using custom scripts, blastn, and blat, we compared miRNAs to identified ApME copies, looking for matches within ApME or within 100 nucleotides of either side. Matches had to meet criteria of >50% sequence similarity and >40% coverage, with at least 10 copies or matching sequences representing 50% of all copies. Manual verification ensures whether a miRNA matches a neighboring copy of a different ApME. Sequences meeting all criteria were considered ApME-miRNA. Then, using the stem-loop method for reverse transcription, miRNA was specifically reverse transcribed.

To verify the existence of ame-mir-3721-3p, we employed a combination of stem-loop reverse transcription (RT) and quantitative PCR (qPCR) methods. The stem-loop RT primer was specifically designed to bind the 3′ end of the mature miRNA, ensuring high specificity for the reverse transcription of ame-mir-3721-3p. The synthesized cDNA was subjected to PCR amplification using a forward primer specific for the mature miRNA sequence and a universal stem-loop reverse primer. To further confirm the specificity of the amplification, the PCR products were analyzed on a 2% agarose gel to verify the presence of a single, distinct band of the expected size. The band was excised and purified for sequencing. Sequencing results were aligned with the predicted ame-mir-3721-3p sequence to confirm its identity. Additionally, the expression levels of ame-mir-3721-3p across different larval stages were measured by RT-qPCR using SYBR Green detection. U6 snRNA was used as the internal control gene due to its stable expression. All primer sequences and PCR conditions are provided in supplementary table S2, Supplementary Material online.

Using RNAfold (Lorenz et al. 2011), we predicted the secondary structures and stability of the 6 identified ApME-miRNAs, calculating the minimum free energy for each possible structure and selecting the lowest-energy structure as the candidate structure. Custom scripts obtained 3′UTR and 5′UTR sequences and positions from genome annotation files. TargetScan, miRanda, and RNAhybrid (Agarwal et al. 2015, Betel et al. 2010, Jan et al. 2006) were used to predict potential target genes of ApME-miRNA, and the intersection of results from all 3 tools was used to select reliable target genes.

Using the selected target genes, we performed network topology analysis with the String database (https://string-db.org/) and Cytoscape software (Shannon et al. 2003), creating a PPI network. Core modules were determined using the MCODE plugin with criteria: MCODE scores > 4, max depth = 100, node score cutoff = 0.3, and k-score = 2. Hub genes were identified using five algorithms in cytoHubba (Chin et al. 2014) (degree, bottleneck, radiality centrality, stress centrality, closeness centrality).

To perform KEGG pathway enrichment analysis on ApME-miRNA target genes, we first downloaded KEGG annotation data for A. mellifera using the AnnotationHub (Morgan et al. 2024) package in R. The gene IDs from the annotation data were converted to gene symbols using appropriate R packages and databases to ensure compatibility with downstream analysis. ApME-miRNA target genes were identified through a combination of prediction algorithms and experimental validation, resulting in a robust and accurate target list. Using the ClusterProfiler (Yu et al. 2012) R package, we performed KEGG pathway enrichment analysis on the identified ApME-miRNA target genes. This involved preparing a gene list of ApME-miRNA targets annotated with their corresponding gene symbols. We then used the enrichKEGG function from ClusterProfiler to calculate the enrichment of KEGG pathways among the target genes, identifying significantly overrepresented pathways compared to the background genome. Statistical significance was assessed using the hypergeometric test implemented in ClusterProfiler's enrichKEGG function, with P-values adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. The results were interpreted to understand the biological pathways and processes potentially regulated by ApME-miRNAs, and visualization tools provided by ClusterProfiler, with bar plots, dot plots, and pathway maps, were utilized to present the enrichment results clearly and comprehensively.

We selected strong and disease-free colonies of A. mellifera. The queen's egg-laying time was marked, and 2-day-old larvae were collected for queen rearing. Every 24 h, queen larvae and worker larvae (from day 1 to day 5) were collected from the queen cups and brood frames, respectively, and stored at −80 °C.

Samples of A. mellifera worker larvae and queen larvae at different ages were collected. RNA was extracted using TRIzol (Accurate Biology, China), and cDNA was synthesized using the Hifair® III 1st Strand cDNA Synthesis SuperMix for qPCR (YESEN, China). The expression levels of miR-3721 and DNMT3 were measured by qRT-PCR (primer sequences listed in supplementary table S2, Supplementary Material online). qRT-PCR was performed using 8-strip tubes (white) (Sangon, China) and the CFX96™ Real-Time System (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA). The qRT-PCR program included an initial denaturation at 95 °C for 30 s, followed by 40 cycles of 95 °C for 5 s, 60 °C for 10 s, and 72 °C for 20 s, with a final extension at 72 °C for 5 min. A melting curve analysis was conducted from 65 to 95 °C. All qRT-PCR experiments were performed in triplicate. Ca was used as an internal reference gene. Gene expression levels were calculated using the 2^-ΔΔCT method, and the data were presented as mean ± SEM. For RNA-Seq differential expression analysis, we accounted for biological variation using established statistical methods designed for multifactor experiments (McCarthy et al. 2012). Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS 22.0 software with t-tests, where *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, and ***P < 0.001.

To determine the binding between miRNA and the 3′UTR of DNMT3, HEK293T cells were cultured in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium (BasalMedia, China) with 10% fetal bovine serum (Moregate Biotech, New Zealand) at 37 °C and 5% CO2. Highly purified plasmid DNA was prepared using the QIAGEN Plasmid Midi Kit (Qiagen, Germany), and miRNA was synthesized by Sangon Biotech (Shanghai, China). Cells were seeded in 24-well plates and, upon reaching 80% to 90% confluence, were transfected with Renilla luciferase vectors and miRNA using a transfection reagent. After 36 to 48 h, luciferase activity was measured using the Dual-Luciferase Reporter Assay System (YESEN, China) to assess the interaction.

We checked the marked brood frames for the queen's egg-laying time and quickly transferred the frames to the laboratory. The 2-day-old larvae were moved into a 48-well culture plate with 40 μL of feed (50% royal jelly, 37% sterile water, 6% glucose, 6% fructose, and 1% yeast extract) (Aupinel et al. 2005) and incubated at 35 °C with 90% humidity for 24 h. The agomir-3721-3p was chemically synthesized by Sangon Biotech (Shanghai, China) as a double-stranded RNA oligonucleotide (sense strand: 5′-UCGUUGAAAAAGAGGAGAAGAU-3′; antisense strand: 5′-AUCUUCUCCUCUUUUCAACGA-3′) with 2′-O-methyl and cholesterol modifications. The negative control agomir (agomir-NC) was designed with a scrambled sequence having no homology to any known honeybee miRNAs and synthesized with identical chemical modifications. The feed containing agomir-3721-3p and agomir-NC was prepared (final concentration 300 nmol/mL). Each 3-day-old larva in the treatment group was fed 40 μL of feed containing agomir-3721-3p, while each larva in the control group was fed 40 μL of feed containing agomir-NC. Larvae were collected at 6, 12, and 18 h postfeeding. Two larvae were placed in an enzyme-free grinding tube as 1 biological replicate, with 3 biological replicates in total. The samples were flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C.

Samples of A. mellifera larvae at different developmental stages were collected. RNA was extracted using TRIzol (Accurate Biology, China), and cDNA was synthesized using the Hifair® III 1st Strand cDNA Synthesis SuperMix for qPCR (YESEN, China). The expression levels of miR-3721, DNMT3, and other relevant genes were measured by qRT-PCR (primer sequences listed in supplementary table S2, Supplementary Material online). qRT-PCR was performed using 8-strip tubes (white) (Sangon, China) and the CFX96™ Real-Time System (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA). The qRT-PCR program included an initial denaturation at 95 °C for 30 s, followed by 40 cycles of 95 °C for 5 s, 60 °C for 10 s, and 72 °C for 20 s, with a final extension at 72 °C for 5 min. A melting curve analysis was conducted from 65 to 95 °C. All qRT-PCR experiments were performed in triplicate. The translation initiation factor calmodulin was used as an internal reference gene. Gene expression levels were calculated using the 2^-ΔΔCT method, and the data were presented as mean ± SEM. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS 22.0 software with t-tests, where *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001.

Strong and healthy colonies of A. mellifera were selected for this study. After marking the timing of queen oviposition, combs containing 1-day-old larvae were promptly transferred to the laboratory. First-instar larvae were grafted using sterilized grafting tools into 48-well plates containing 60 μL of prewarmed artificial diet (34 °C, 20 min). The diet consisted of 50% royal jelly, 25% sterile water, 12% glucose, 12% fructose, and 1% yeast extract. The plates were maintained in an incubator at 34 °C with 85% relative humidity for 8 h.

For experimental treatment, artificial diet containing agomir-3721 or agomir-NC (final concentration 300 nmol/mL) was prepared and prewarmed at 34 °C for 20 min before use. From day 1 to day 3, larvae in the treatment group received 50 μL fresh diet containing agomir-3721 daily, while the control group received 50 μL fresh diet containing agomir-NC. On day 4, larvae were transferred to 24-well plates containing 150 μL of prewarmed corresponding diet. The plates were maintained under the same conditions, with 150 μL fresh diet provided daily.

After 7 to 8 d of larval rearing, larvae began defecating white cottony excrement and yellow uric acid crystals, indicating the onset of pupation. The larvae were then transferred onto UV-sterilized lens cleaning papers in 6-well plates to remove moisture and excrement. The plates were maintained at 34 °C with 85% relative humidity, with cleaning papers replaced daily for the first 3 d. Larvae were allowed to complete pupation naturally until emergence.

Body weight of newly emerged bees was measured individually using an electronic balance. Abdominal tissues were dissected and observed under a Stereozoom S9E stereomicroscope. Ovarian measurements and images were captured using a DFC7000T(11547106)BZ01 fluorescence microscope with LAS-X software.

Abdominal tissues from newly emerged bees of both treatment and control groups were collected for RNA extraction using TRIzol reagent (Accurate Biology, China). The extracted RNA was reverse transcribed using Hifair® III 1st Strand cDNA Synthesis SuperMix for qPCR (YESEN, China). Expression levels of Vg and VgR genes were analyzed by qRT-PCR using 8-strip white tubes (Sangon Biotech, China) and CFX96™ Real-Time System (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA). The qRT-PCR program consisted of 95 °C for 30 s, followed by 40 cycles of 95 °C for 5 s, 60 °C for 10 s, and 72 °C for 20 s, with a final extension at 72 °C for 5 min. Melting curve analysis was performed from 65 to 95 °C.

All qRT-PCR experiments were performed in triplicate with calmodulin as the internal reference gene. Relative gene expression was calculated using the 2-ΔΔCT method. Data are presented as mean ± SEM, and statistical analysis was performed using SPSS 22.0 software with Student's t-test (*P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, and ***P < 0.001).

title: Nourishment level affects caste-related gene expression in Polistes wasps
abstract: BackgroundSocial insects exhibit striking phenotypic plasticity in the form of distinct reproductive (queen) and non-reproductive (worker) castes, which are typically driven by differences in the environment during early development. Nutritional environment and nourishment during development has been shown to be broadly associated with caste determination across social insect taxa such as bees, wasps, and termites. In primitively social insects such as Polistes paper wasps, caste remains flexible throughout adulthood, but there is evidence that nourishment inequalities can bias caste development with workers receiving limited nourishment compared to queens. Dominance and vibrational signaling are behaviors that have also been linked to caste differences in paper wasps, suggesting that a combination of nourishment and social factors may drive caste determination. To better understand the molecular basis of nutritional effects on caste determination, we used RNA-sequencing to investigate the gene expression changes in response to proteinaceous nourishment deprivation in Polistes metricus larvae.ResultsWe identified 285 nourishment-responsive transcripts, many of which are related to lipid metabolism and oxidation-reduction activity. Via comparisons to previously identified caste-related genes, we found that nourishment restriction only partially biased wasp gene expression patterns toward worker caste-like traits, which supports the notion that nourishment, in conjunction with social environment, is a determinant of developmental caste bias. In addition, we conducted cross-species comparisons of nourishment-responsive genes, and uncovered largely lineage-specific gene expression changes, suggesting few shared nourishment-responsive genes across taxa.ConclusionOverall, the results from this study highlight the complex and multifactorial nature of environmental effects on the gene expression patterns underlying plastic phenotypes.Electronic supplementary materialThe online version of this article (doi:10.1186/s12864-015-1410-y) contains supplementary material, which is available to authorized users.
body_text:
Phenotypic plasticity provides an important adaptive mechanism by which morphology, physiology, and/or behavior can be adjusted to biotic and abiotic environmental factors including temperature, nutrition, population density, and predator presence [1]. There are a number of striking examples of phenotypic plasticity in insects: dimorphic horn development in dung beetles [2], seasonal color polyphenism in butterflies [3], and wing polyphenism in aphids (reviewed in [4]). One of the best-studied models of insect phenotypic plasticity is reproductive castes in social insects, especially social Hymenoptera (bees, ants, and wasps [5]). In most social insects, genotypic differences do not account for differences between reproductive (queen) and non-reproductive (worker) castes (reviewed in [6]). Instead, environmental factors induce differences in hormone titers and gene expression (reviewed in [6]), leading to the development of queens or workers, which vary in physiology and behavior and for advanced social species, in morphology [5].

One particular environmental factor, food availability, is especially important for caste polyphenism in social insects. Differential nourishment [7-10] and nutrition-related genes and pathways (e.g. storage proteins such as vitellogenin and hexamerin, insulin/insulin-like signaling (IIS) pathways) have been linked to caste differences in honey bees [11,12], paper wasps [13,14], and termites [15,16]. This suggests that the influence of nutrition on caste formation may be broadly shared across diverse taxa [17]. There have been numerous studies investigating the molecular mechanisms underlying queen-worker caste determination in advanced eusocial species, especially honey bees [18-25]. In honey bees, nutritional differences for larvae fed either royal jelly or worker jelly precede a developmental switch resulting in alternative caste phenotypes [26]. Nutrition is also important for caste differences in primitively eusocial species, which lack morphological castes, but we know much less about the molecular mechanisms that underlie the formation of their more subtle behavioral and physiological castes. In primitively eusocial species such as paper wasps, differential nourishment does not strictly determine caste but can lead to a caste bias, whereby female larvae that are fed larger quantities of food are more likely to be future reproductive queens (called “gynes”) as adults [27]. However, the ultimate caste fate of a female is decided during adulthood. First-brood offspring of an established nest are capable of independent reproduction, but instead they perform allomaternal care (worker behavior) as a response to cues emitted by larvae in the nest [28]. Subsequent social reinforcement of worker behavior often occurs via dominance behaviors by the queen or other workers [29,30].

Primitively eusocial taxa such as Polistes are an informative group for understanding the evolution of eusociality and the origins of castes [31,32]. Across the annual colony cycle of primitively social wasps in the genus Polistes¸ the quantity of larval nourishment changes according to seasonal changes in the adult-to-larva ratio [10,27]. First-brood offspring produced early in the colony cycle have been reared by a single nest-founding queen or few queens, which also perform all colony tasks such as nest building, foraging, egg laying, and brood rearing [30]. At this early time in the colony cycle the adult-to-larva ratio is low [30,33], which leads to low feeding rates and more limited larval nourishment compared to offspring reared by workers and produced later in the colony cycle (future queens or “gynes”). Physiological evidence of nourishment-related differences between workers and gynes collected from naturally-founded colonies in the field include greater fat body stores in gynes [34,35], greater quantities of the storage protein hexamerin 1 in gynes [36,37], and greater quantities of four additional proteins in gynes [14]. Experimental studies show that nourishment inequalities that correspond to early-season and late-season larval development contexts are associated with development of offspring having characteristics of worker and gyne phenotypes, respectively [38,39].

In addition to the established role of nourishment in caste differences in Polistes, social factors, such as dominance behavior [29,31] and maternal influences [40-42] also play a role. Jeanne and Suryanarayanan [40] propose a hypothesis for caste determination in primitively social wasps that incorporates not only nourishment variability, but also social environmental inputs from maternal care, specifically vibrational signals called antennal drumming. Antennal drumming may be an example of a maternal manipulation [43] that directs larvae toward a worker developmental trajectory, and this effect may interact with nourishment induced changes in caste phenotype. Thus, nourishment is likely to act in concert with social environmental factors in determining differences in gyne and worker caste development in Polistes.

In this study, we investigated the effect of experimental proteinaceous nourishment deprivation during larval development on caste-related gene expression in a primitively eusocial species, the paper wasp Polistes metricus. We had three main goals. First, we explored the transcriptional responses of wasp larvae to high and low nourishment levels during laboratory rearing using RNA-sequencing. Second, we tested the hypothesis that nourishment level relates to caste-related gene expression; specifically that low nourishment is associated with more worker-like gene expression patterns, and high nourishment is associated with more gyne-like expression patterns. To do this, we compared nourishment differential expression to a set of nearly 800 previously identified genes associated with caste development in field-reared P. metricus [13], and we did so on multiple levels: individual transcripts, pathways and biological functions. Third, we tested whether the molecular mechanisms underlying the response to nourishment are conserved across taxa by comparing our results to two other nourishment deprivation studies in fruit flies [44] and dung beetles [45]. Our overall goal was to better understand the extent and nature of the role of nourishment and nourishment-related genes in caste development in a primitively social wasp species.

To assess differential gene expression, we mapped reads to a previously assembled de novo transcriptome for P. metricus; the transcriptome was based on both the sequence data described here in conjunction with additional samples described in a previous study [13]. By comparing expression patterns from head samples from 8 individual wasp larvae under high and low nourishment, we identified 284 P. metricus differentially expressed transcripts (DETs) that differed between low and high nourishment treatments, using DESeq (FDR ≤ 0.05, [46]), heretofore referred to as “P. metricus nourishment-responsive DETs”. Of these DETs, 207 (72.9%) were upregulated in low compared to high nourishment larvae (Figure 1 is a heat map of the scaled DET read counts across P. metricus nourishment samples. Additional file 1 includes the list of P. metricus nourishment-responsive DETs). One important feature of these results is the presence of outlier individuals, i.e. one individual low nourishment larva clustered with the high nourishment samples and a high nourishment larva clustered with the low nourishment samples (Figure 1). The variability of gene expression amongst biological samples is not completely surprising; our previous work has found high inter-individual variation in gene expression [13], effects of lab rearing (JM Jandt, JL Thomson, AC Geffre, AL Toth: Rearing environment may bias social traits: A case study with Polistes wasps, submitted), and variable effects of nourishment level on physiology [38].

It is important to validate RNA-Seq data using another method such as quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR). However, for this study, we had limited samples and quantities of RNA [38], so we could not perform qRT-PCR validation on actual samples from this experiment. In lieu of the sample limitations, we instead made a comparison to pre-existing data on nourishment-responsive expression patterns from adult brains of P. metricus under starved vs. ad lib food conditions [47]. Although not ideal because of differences in tissue type and life stage, this comparison still provides a useful point of comparison to validate whether the expression patterns uncovered in this RNA-Seq study are robust.

Of 24 candidate genes, Daugherty et al. [47] identified 10 genes with differential expression in adult P. metricus brains reared under low and high nourishment conditions using qRT-PCR. We tested for a correlation (Spearman) in the log2 fold changes between the 24 candidate genes from Daugherty et al. [47] and the orthologous transcripts in this study, i.e. best BLAST hits between the primer sequences from Daugherty et al. [47] and the P. metricus transcriptome (Additional file 2: Figure S3 is a visual representation of the log2 fold changes for both studies; Additional file 3 lists the log2 fold change for each gene/transcript and the directionality for differentially expressed genes). For some genes, there is more than one best BLAST hit to the P. metricus transcriptome, so all transcripts were used for the correlation analysis. The gene PmTOR is absent from the P. metricus transcriptome, so this gene was removed from the analysis. Although none of the orthologous transcripts are significantly differentially expressed in the RNA-seq study, we nonetheless identified a significant positive correlation in log2 fold changes between these two studies (Spearman ρ: 0.54, p-value = 0.001), which provides support for our observed RNA-Seq results.

One reason we may not have observed statistically significant differential expression of these candidate genes in the RNA-Seq study, despite the strong correlation with the qRT-PCR data, is because of the limited statistical power. Differential expression calls are more stringent in this RNA-Seq study compared to the qRT-PCR analysis because familywise error correction is more severe due to the larger number of genes (over 75,000 compared to 24 genes). Furthermore, the qRT-PCR study has a larger sample size (n = 47) compared to the RNA-Seq study (n = 8), which provides greater statistical power for detecting differential expression.

Next, we investigated how P. metricus nourishment-responsive DETs compared to caste-related gene expression. A previous study [13] compared gene expression in field-collected, early season (worker-destined) larvae to late season (gyne-destined) larvae, and identified 736 caste-related DETs. Both low nourishment (described above) and worker-destined larvae [13] show a pronounced bias towards upregulated gene expression (72.9% upregulated in low nourishment and 91.7% upregulated in worker-destined larvae). This pattern generally agrees with the prediction that worker-destined and nourishment-deprived larvae have similar transcriptional states.

There was a statistically significant but relatively small overlap (43 transcripts) between the nourishment-responsive and caste-related DETs (Chi-square with Yates’ correction: p < 0.0001). Of these shared DETs, the directionality of gene expression change was unexpected: eight (18.6%) were upregulated in low nourishment larvae compared to high nourishment larvae, whereas 38 (88.4%) were upregulated in worker-destined larvae relative to queen-destined larvae (see Figure 2a for a Venn diagram of the number of unique and overlapping caste and nourishment-responsive DETs, Additional file 2: Figure S1 for a heatmap of the overlapping caste and nourishment-responsive DETs, and Additional file 4 for the list of overlapping DETs). To further explore these data beyond examining an overlap of gene lists, we performed a combined statistical analysis of data from both the nourishment level and caste contrasts, and the results also indicate some overlap in gene expression patterns across the two studies (see Methods, with complete description of the approach and results in Additional file 2 and Additional file 5). Our previous study suggested gene expression similarity across studies is more pronounced on the level of pathways and gene functional categories, rather than specific genes or transcripts [13]. Therefore, we also examined our data at the level of pathways using the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) [48,49]. Using best BLAST hits to D. melanogaster, very few transcripts (799 = 1.0% of the transcriptome) were annotated with enzyme codes for the KEGG analysis with Blast2GO [50] (see Additional file 1 for a list of transcripts annotated with enzyme codes by KEGG pathway). The presence of many transcripts without homology is a shortcoming of the dataset, but is expected and standard for Illumina-based data from non-model species [51]. Only 7% (20) of the nourishment DETs were known members of KEGG pathways, therefore we identified very few (7 of 118) KEGG pathways with at least one DET. We then looked to see if these seven pathways were also related to caste differences [13]. Four of the seven pathways also had caste-related DETs (including glycerolipid metabolism, nitrogen metabolism, and purine metabolism; listed in Additional file 4), but this amount of overlap was not statistically significant (Fisher’s exact test, p-value = 0.12). The majority of the DETs are upregulated in both low nourishment and worker-destined larvae for all four of these shared KEGG pathways (Figure 2b is a Venn diagram of the number of KEGG pathways with nourishment and/or caste DETs), which is in agreement with the prediction that nourishment-responsive biochemical pathways are regulated in a similar direction to what is found between castes in paper wasps.

On the level of gene functional categories, fifty-two GO terms were significantly enriched within the P. metricus nourishment-responsive DETs compared to the remainder of transcriptome (Figure 3; Additional file 1 includes the list of enriched GO terms). These included functions related to lipoprotein metabolism, oxidation reduction activity, and polysaccharide metabolism. More than 30% of GO terms (including terms related to oxidoreductase activity and carbohydrate metabolism) were common to both caste- and nourishment manipulation-related DETs, representing a significant overlap (Chi-square test with Yates’ correction, p < 0.0001; Figure 2b; Additional file 4 lists the shared caste and nourishment enriched GO terms). Because nourishment is an important driver of phenotypic plasticity in many species, we were interested in determining whether the molecular mechanisms underlying the response to nourishment identified in paper wasps are conserved in other taxa. After an extensive literature search, we identified two studies from other insects that also examined transcriptional responses to nutritional stress: 1) a microarray study of tissue-specific (fat body and muscle) gene expression derived from fruit fly larvae [44] and 2) a microarray study of thoracic horn development in female dung beetle pupae [45]. Although not ideal comparisons to our paper wasp dataset because of differences in life stages and sampled tissues, these studies still provide useful preliminary comparisons to begin addressing whether there are any conserved of nourishment-responsive transcripts.
